section_titles: As a class organisation we would like to harmonise how the R
text:
As a class organisation we would like to harmonise how the Racing Committee provides information to competitors via VHF during a yacht race.

There is a long history of using the VHF during race starts. Ever since sea going yachts were obliged to be equipped with a VHF radio, it has been used in various manners to provide competitors with information during a race.

The following protocol guides the RC in the efficient execution of VHF communication.

Protocol:

Selection of a VHF channel depends on the location of the race. Use one of the inter-ship channels (i.e. 72, 8, 77) and check the channel for the presence of other users in the vicinity of the course. The VHF channel must be specified in the Sailing Instructions.
The starting vessel sails to the starting area and reports its position. The way in which the position is reported is not strictly defined, but must be clear. So use for instance either latitude/longitude or bearing/distance to inform the competitors.
Once in position, the starting vessel will broadcast a time check at set intervals and repeats its position. The time checks start one hour prior to the start, so the competitors can synchronize their watches/clocks.
When starting times differ from the starting times published in the SI, the RC shall broadcast the expected starting time 30 minutes and 15 minutes before each start. This goes also for any subsequent starts on the same day.
The RC will count down in useful intervals to the 5 minute mark before the warning signal of the first start. The final 5 seconds will be counted in the following manner: “5, 4, 3, 2, 1, TOP”.
The warning signal and the start of each class will be counted down in the same manner.
After the warning signal (5 minutes prior to the start) the competitors will be informed which signals have been displayed on the starting vessel:
The class flag(s) for the upcoming start.
Number of laps in a W/L course.
Heading and distance to the first mark.
When for any reason the race is postponed (AP flag) or abandoned (N flag) during the starting procedure, the RC will inform the competitors of this event by broadcasting “The start has been aborted” and will give further information (such as new starting time) as soon as possible.
When all boats are clear of the line following the starting signal, make the call “All clear”.
When at the starting signal the RC is unable to identify the boats that are OCS, the First Substitute is hoisted with two sounds and a “General recall” is broadcast over VHF
In the case of an individual recall the flag X is hoisted with one sound. On the VHF the message will be “X-Ray for n boats” followed as soon as possible - preferably within one minute - by the sailnumbers of and/or names of the boats that are OCS. After a boat has sailed completely over the pre-start side of the starting line, this boat will be informed that “sailnumber x is clear”. When the last boat clears the line, an “All yachts are clear” is broadcast.
During the race the RC will monitor the VHF channel for messages from competitors, such as retirements or requests for assistance in case of emergency.
Changes to the course or shortening of the race can be communicated via VHF, but competitors may have turned off their VHF because of the distraction of unnecessary communication during the race (such as the start of the next class). Therefore always use the combination of the prescribed visual/audible signals to communicate with the competitors.
Why this protocol?

Although the principle seems simple, use of the VHF during races has given numerous RCs a lot of headaches. The fear of giving incorrect information over the VHF, leading to successful protests by competitors, leaves some Race Officers reluctant to use it. Ask most competitors and you will hear how much they value VHF information during the start. A well-executed VHF Protocol gives pre-start confidence to the competitors, and helps prevent early starts and possible subsequent disqualifications. The VHF Protocol below has been written with the guidance of competitors with international experience, since the use of VHF is standard procedure in major international races.

Advantages of a standard protocol

By making use of a standard protocol, competitors can rely on correct and timely broadcast of relevant information. This prevents unnecessary questions from competitors via VHF, which can be quite annoying for both the RC and other competitors. The standard protocol can be tailored to fit local needs, but the communication needs to remain predictable.

For competitors, an external loudspeaker or handheld VHF is necessary to maximize the availability and benefit of the information that will be broadcast by the RC.

Flags have priority over VHF

The procedures for the proper race conduct are defined in Part 3 of the “Racing Rules of Sailing” (RRS). The RRS specifies that race signals can be given by a combination of visual and sound signals. Absence of a sound signal shall be disregarded and times shall be taken from the visual signal.

Depending on the size of the boats or the length of the starting line the signals on the starting vessel can be difficult to see or hear. Therefore internationally it is now standard practice to use VHF as an additional means of communicating the (pre)start signals. With regards to Part 3 of the RRS, the VHF does not replace or supersede the visual and sound signals on board the starting vessel and problems with or absence of VHF communications cannot be grounds for redress.

PS: This protocol has been created to standardise VHF communication during yacht races. Communication with the competitors shall be brief and to the point, but friendly and never condescending. The competitors shall be asked to refrain from using the designated channel as this might interfere with the starting procedure and possibly annoy other competitors. As RC you can help avoid unnecessary questions over the VHF by following this protocol.

text: Summary The Recommendation describes the technical characteristics of VHF radiotelephone transmitters and receivers (or transceivers) used in the maritime mobile service when operating in 25 kHz channels of Appendix S18 [Appendix 18] of the Radio Regulations (RR). It also contains those additional characteristics of transceivers required to operate digital selective calling. The ITU Radiocommunication Assembly, considering a)that Resolution No. 308 of the World Administrative Radio Conference (Geneva, 1979) stipulated that: –all maritime mobile VHF radiotelephone equipment shall conform to 25 kHz standards by 1 January 1983; b)that RR Appendix S18 [Appendix 18] gives a table of transmitting frequencies which is based upon the principle of 25 kHz channel separations for the maritime mobile service; c)that in Opinion 42, the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) has been invited to advise the ITU Radiocommunication Sector of any methods of measurement applicable to radio equipment used in land mobile services; and that such methods of measurement may also be suitable for radio equipment used in maritime mobile services; d)that there is a need to specify the technical characteristics of VHF radiotelephone equipment operating in the maritime mobile service in channels spaced by 25 kHz, recommends 1that the following characteristics should be met by VHF (metric) FM radiotelephone equipment used for the maritime mobile services operating on the frequencies specified in RR Appendix S18 [Appendix 18].

text: a)sensing to determine the presence of a signal on 156.525 MHz (channel 70); and b)automatic prevention of the transmission of a call, except for distress and safety calls, when the channel is occupied by calls. 1.2Transmitters 6 1.2.1The frequency tolerance for coast station transmitters should not exceed 5 parts in 10, and that for ship station 6 transmitters should not exceed 10 parts in 10. 1.2.2Spurious emissions on discrete frequencies, when measured in a non-reactive load equal to the nominal output impedance of the transmitter, should be in accordance with the provisions of RR Appendix S3 [Appendix 8]. 1.2.3The carrier power for coast stations should not normally exceed 50 W. 1.2.4The carrier power for ship station transmitters should not exceed 25 W. Means should be provided to readily reduce this power to 1 W or less for use at short ranges, except for digital selective calling equipment operating on 156.525 MHz (channel 70) in which case the power reduction facility is optional (see also Recommen- dation ITU-R M.541 recommends 3.7). 1.2.5The upper limit of the audio-frequency band should not exceed 3 kHz. m 1.2.6The cabinet radiated power should not exceed 25 W. text: The examples below show exactly what to transmit, word for word, for common routine communications, correct procedure-word usage, and urgency (PAN PAN) calls. Each example first explains the situation, then gives the precise transmission an operator should use. chapter_title: Routine, Procedure-Word And Urgency Call Demonstrations
text:
To open a routine call to another vessel, state the called station's name twice, then your own station's name twice, then invite a reply. Example: "SEA OTTER, SEA OTTER, THIS IS NORTHERN STAR, NORTHERN STAR, OVER." The double repetition of each name reduces the chance of a mis-heard call sign on a noisy channel.

To open a routine call to a harbour or port control, use the same double-repeat structure and immediately say what you want. Example: "PORT CONTROL, PORT CONTROL, THIS IS MV AMBER TIDE, MV AMBER TIDE, REQUESTING PERMISSION TO ENTER, OVER."

chapter_title: Routine, Procedure-Word And Urgency Call Demonstrations
text:
A concise routine call includes only identity, timing or position, and the single action requested, then closes cleanly. Example: "LOCK CONTROL, THIS IS BLUE FALCON, TWO MINUTES OUT, LOCK ONE, PERMISSION TO ENTER, OVER." On reply: "BLUE FALCON, THIS IS LOCK CONTROL, ROGER, LOCK ONE, OUT." Nothing beyond identity, timing, and the one request is included; this is the standard for routine calls under the SMCP.

Another concise example, requesting a berth: "HARBOUR MASTER, THIS IS SILVER GULL, REQUEST BERTH ASSIGNMENT, OVER." Reply: "SILVER GULL, THIS IS HARBOUR MASTER, BERTH FOUR, OVER." Close: "HARBOUR MASTER, THIS IS SILVER GULL, ROGER, BERTH FOUR, OUT."

chapter_title: Routine, Procedure-Word And Urgency Call Demonstrations
text:
When a routine communication carries operationally important information, such as pilotage advice, it must be logged with UTC time, the channel used, the other station's name, a factual summary of the advice given, any instruction to change channel, and confirmation that the message was read back. Example log entry: "1430 UTC, Channel 12, SOLENT VTS advised recommended course 270, holding position off Fairway Buoy, tidal window closes 1600, instructed to monitor Channel 12, advice read back and confirmed."

A second logging example, for a traffic report: "0915 UTC, Channel 71, DOVER COASTGUARD reported inbound traffic in the Dover Strait, TSS crossing recommended at 090 degrees, instructed to report position again at the Varne buoy, message read back and confirmed."

chapter_title: Routine, Procedure-Word And Urgency Call Demonstrations
text:
After the substantive exchange is complete, close by stating which channel you will now monitor, then say OUT. Example: "STORM PETREL, THIS IS CRIMSON WAVE, STANDING BY ON CHANNEL SIXTEEN, OUT." If returning to the international calling and distress channel: "STORM PETREL, THIS IS CRIMSON WAVE, RETURNING TO CHANNEL ONE-SIX, OUT."

The pro-words OVER and OUT are never used together. OVER means a reply is expected; OUT means the exchange is finished and no reply is expected. Saying "OVER AND OUT" is a common error and is never correct procedure, because it contradicts itself: it invites a reply while also announcing that none is expected.

section_titles: Requesting A Channel Change During A Routine Call
text: To move a routine conversation off the calling channel, state the proposed working channel and wait for acknowledgement before switching. Example: "GOLDEN TERN, THIS IS MISTY HARBOR, SWITCH CHANNEL SEVENTY-THREE, OVER." Reply: "MISTY HARBOR, THIS IS GOLDEN TERN, CHANNEL SEVENTY-THREE, OVER." Both stations then move to Channel 73 before continuing.

chapter_title: Routine, Procedure-Word And Urgency Call Demonstrations
section_titles: Routine Position And Traffic Reporting To A VTS
text: When reporting to a Vessel Traffic Service on request, give vessel name, position, course, speed, and destination in that order, then invite further instruction. Example: "THAMES VTS, THIS IS WINDWARD ISLE, POSITION FIVE ONE DECIMAL FOUR ZERO NORTH ZERO ZERO DECIMAL TWO EIGHT EAST, COURSE ZERO NINE ZERO, SPEED TWELVE KNOTS, BOUND FOR TILBURY, OVER." Reply: "WINDWARD ISLE, THIS IS THAMES VTS, ROGER, REPORT AGAIN AT NORTHFLEET, OUT."

chapter_title: Routine, Procedure-Word And Urgency Call Demonstrations
text:
The pro-word I SPELL introduces a letter-by-letter phonetic spelling of a word already spoken in plain language, and the plain word is repeated once more afterward so the listener can confirm it. Example: "THIS IS COPPER KESTREL, DESTINATION SCHEVENINGEN, I SPELL SIERRA CHARLIE HOTEL ECHO VICTOR ECHO NOVEMBER INDIA NOVEMBER GOLF ECHO NOVEMBER, SCHEVENINGEN, OVER."

A second example, spelling a vessel name during a routine identification: "THIS IS OCEAN FALCON, I SPELL OSCAR CHARLIE ECHO ALPHA NOVEMBER, FOXTROT ALPHA LIMA CHARLIE OSCAR NOVEMBER, OCEAN FALCON, OVER."

chapter_title: Routine, Procedure-Word And Urgency Call Demonstrations
text:
The pro-word CORRECTION explicitly voids whatever was just said and signals that the corrected version follows immediately, within the same transmission. Example: "THIS IS RAVENSBROOK, MY POSITION IS FIVE ZERO ONE TWO DECIMAL FIVE NORTH, ZERO ZERO ONE FOUR FIVE DECIMAL THREE WEST, CORRECTION, ZERO ZERO ONE FOUR FIVE DECIMAL THREE EAST, OVER."

A second CORRECTION example: "THIS IS DUNCAIRN, REQUESTING BERTH SIX, CORRECTION, BERTH SIXTEEN, OVER." The corrected figure always comes immediately after the word CORRECTION, never as a separate follow-up transmission.

chapter_title: Routine, Procedure-Word And Urgency Call Demonstrations
text:
SAY AGAIN is used to request a repeat of all or part of a message, and should specify exactly what is unclear whenever possible. Example: "THIS IS HARTSHAVEN, YOUR SIGNAL IS UNREADABLE, SAY AGAIN YOUR ENTIRE MESSAGE, OVER." A more specific version: "THIS IS EASTMERE, YOUR SIGNAL IS BROKEN, SAY AGAIN ALL AFTER POSITION, OVER."

When responding to a SAY AGAIN request, repeat the requested information slowly and without paraphrasing, digit by digit if it is numerical. Example: "THIS IS FENHOLM, I SAY AGAIN, MY POSITION IS FIVE ZERO DECIMAL ONE TWO MINUTES NORTH, PERSONS ON BOARD FIVE, I SAY AGAIN, PERSONS ON BOARD FIVE, OVER."

chapter_title: Routine, Procedure-Word And Urgency Call Demonstrations
text: ROGER means the previous transmission was received and understood; it does not mean agreement or compliance. WILCO means "I have received your message, understood it, and will comply." Example exchange: "THIS IS CRAGMOUTH, PROCEED TO ANCHORAGE BRAVO, OVER." Reply: "THIS IS ASHWORTH BAY, WILCO, OVER." A separate example where only acknowledgement, not compliance, is intended: "THIS IS GREYWATER POINT, ROGER, OVER."

chapter_title: Routine, Procedure-Word And Urgency Call Demonstrations
text:
AFFIRMATIVE means yes; NEGATIVE means no. Both are used instead of a plain "yes" or "no" because they are less likely to be misheard over a noisy channel. Example: "THIS IS MAINSTAY, CONFIRM YOU ARE MAKING WAY, OVER." Reply: "THIS IS OUTER LEDGE, AFFIRMATIVE, MAKING WAY AT SIX KNOTS, OVER." A NEGATIVE example: "THIS IS NORTH RACE, CONFIRM DECK CARGO SECURE, OVER." Reply: "THIS IS WHISTLING ROCK, NEGATIVE, SECURING NOW, OVER."

The Distinction Between OVER And OUT

OVER hands the transmission to the other station and invites a reply. OUT ends the exchange and states that no reply is expected. A station never says both together. Correct mid-conversation use: "THIS IS MID CHANNEL, REQUEST YOUR INTENTIONS, OVER." Correct conversation-ending use: "THIS IS FAIRWAY GATE, INTENTIONS UNDERSTOOD, OUT."

chapter_title: Routine, Procedure-Word And Urgency Call Demonstrations
section_titles: Full PAN PAN Urgency Call Structure
text:
A formal urgency call begins with the urgency signal spoken three times, followed by ALL STATIONS spoken three times, then the vessel's identity spoken three times, then MMSI, position, the nature of the urgency, and a request for assistance. Example: "PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS SKYWARD NINE, SKYWARD NINE, SKYWARD NINE, MMSI TWO THREE FIVE ZERO ZERO ONE TWO THREE FOUR, POSITION FIVE ZERO DECIMAL TWO NORTH, ZERO ZERO ONE DECIMAL FIVE WEST, LOSS OF STEERING GEAR, DRIFTING WITH WIND TOWARDS THE COAST AT FOUR KNOTS, AMPLE SEA ROOM AT PRESENT, FOUR PERSONS ON BOARD, REQUESTING ASSISTANCE OR A TOW, OVER."

A second full urgency example for an engine failure adrift: "PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS TRIDENT LINE, TRIDENT LINE, TRIDENT LINE, MMSI TWO THREE FIVE ONE ONE TWO TWO ONE ONE, POSITION FOUR NINE DECIMAL EIGHT NORTH, ZERO ZERO TWO DECIMAL ONE EAST, TOTAL ENGINE FAILURE, DRIFTING, NO IMMEDIATE DANGER, TWO PERSONS ON BOARD, REQUESTING TOW ASSISTANCE, OVER."

A third full urgency example for a person requiring medical attention that is not immediately life-threatening: "PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS COASTAL GUARDIAN, COASTAL GUARDIAN, COASTAL GUARDIAN, MMSI TWO THREE FOUR NINE NINE NINE ZERO ZERO ONE, POSITION FIVE ONE DECIMAL ONE NORTH, ZERO ZERO ONE DECIMAL THREE EAST, CREW MEMBER WITH SUSPECTED BROKEN LIMB, CONSCIOUS AND STABLE, THREE PERSONS ON BOARD, REQUESTING MEDICAL ADVICE, OVER."

chapter_title: Routine, Procedure-Word And Urgency Call Demonstrations
section_titles: Checking Whether A Situation Warrants An Urgency Call
text: If unsure whether a situation is serious enough for a formal PAN PAN, call the coastguard first on their working channel and ask for advice rather than escalating immediately. Example: "SOLENT COASTGUARD, THIS IS PELAGIC, ROUTINE, REQUEST ADVICE, OVER." After describing the situation factually, the coastguard will advise whether to declare a formal urgency call, continue monitoring, or stand down. This avoids both over-reacting and under-reacting to a developing situation.

Example: "THIS IS NORSECREST, I SAY AGAIN, MY POSITION IS FIVE ZERO DECIMAL ONE TWO MINUTES NORTH, PERSONS ON BOARD FIVE, I SAY AGAIN, PERSONS ON BOARD FIVE, OVER." The voluntary use of I SAY AGAIN for safety-critical facts, even before being asked, is good practice.

section_titles: Urgency Call After A Person Overboard Has Been Recovered Safely
text: Once a person overboard has been recovered unharmed, a PAN PAN cancellation or "all clear" broadcast should follow so other stations do not continue diverting resources. Example: "ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS OCEANEX, OCEANEX, OCEANEX, PAN PAN CANCEL, PERSON OVERBOARD RECOVERED SAFELY, NO FURTHER ASSISTANCE REQUIRED, OUT."

[Urgency Call After A Person Overboard Has Been Recovered Safely — warning]
Once a person overboard has been recovered unharmed, a PAN PAN cancellation or "all clear" broadcast should follow so other stations do not continue diverting resources. Example: "ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS OCEANEX, OCEANEX, OCEANEX, PAN PAN CANCEL, PERSON OVERBOARD RECOVERED SAFELY, NO FURTHER ASSISTANCE REQUIRED, OUT."

chapter_title: Sailing Basics: How To Use A Vhf Radio
section_titles: My brothers and I grew up in a…
text:
My brothers and I grew up in a sailing family. We had a 27-foot Catalina that we’d take out on the weekends any time the weather was nice and even when the weather wasn’t nice, we’d often still find ourselves on the boat, helping to scrub the decks and maintain the gear. On those days, we’d inevitably get bored, at which point the VHF radio would become a serious temptation. One day, when our dad was occupied somewhere on the bow, I grabbed the radio and said something silly. Before I could crack another joke, my dad was over top of me, grabbing the receiver out of my hand. I never knew he could move that fast! I learned the importance of VHF radio etiquette that day, and it’s a lesson I’ve never forgotten.

Your VHF radio is your best way to communicate with other boats on the water, with marinas, and with the coast guard, if necessary. VHF stands for “Very High Frequency.” It’s the standard form of communication on the water, is more reliable than cell phones, and it’s always being monitored. Learning to use it, however, is a little like learning a new language. You can’t just hop on and start talking.

Below are the basics, and you can learn VHF usage in-depth in NauticEd’s Bareboat Charter Clinic.

Always be listening
Using a VHF marine radioYour VHF radio is a safety tool. Even if you don’t need to communicate with anyone, you should be listening for important weather updates and other announcements on channel 16. This is especially true if you’re boating in high-traffic areas or locations where weather can change quickly. You don’t have to have it blaring beside you and not let anyone else on the boat speak (not exactly our idea of a good sail), but you’ll want to have it on while you’re in transit.

And note there are certain regulations that require you to keep a “Radio Watch” at all times. The rules state that in general, any vessel equipped with a VHF marine radiotelephone must maintain a watch on channel 16 (156.8MHz) whenever the radiotelephone is not being used to communicate.

Brush up on your VHF lingo
VHF communication has its own set of terms that have developed over the last century. These were originally brief, clear words and ideas that could be easily transmitted over telegraph. As vocal communication developed, these terms continued to develop and were used to keep communications brief and to avoid confusion and miscommunication. These terms are often called “procedure words,” or “prowords.” You can find exhaustive lists online, but here are a few basic ones that are good to know.

chapter_title: Sailing Basics: How To Use A Vhf Radio
text:
There are three different levels of safety or distress calls, which boaters can use to let other boats in the area know of potential or real danger. Distress calls are initiated on Channel 16 (and a reason you always monitor it).  If you hear or receive a distress call and cannot assist, immediately cease all transmission on Channel 16! Any vessel with knowledge of distress traffic who cannot assist is forbidden from transmitting on a distress channel (until you receive the “all clear”).

MAYDAY: This is an urgent and immediate distress call, made when a boat is in danger of sinking or there is a fire, man overboard, or medical emergency on board. Vessels that are close enough to help are required to do so. You should only make a mayday call if you are in serious or immediate danger. Below is the generally accepted procedure for a Channel 16 Mayday:

If you have a VHF marine radio, tune it to channel 16. Unless you know you are outside VHF range of shore and ships, call on channel 16 first.
A Mayday distress signal is first spoken three times, “MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY”.
The words “THIS IS”, spoken once.
Name of the vessel in distress (spoken three times) and call sign or boat registration number, spoken once. *TIP: have this information written and nearby the VHF for anyone onboard calling a mayday. Seconds count in an emergency!
Repeat “MAYDAY” and name of vessel, spoken once.
Give position of the vessel by latitude or longitude or by bearing (true or magnetic, state which) and distance to a well-known landmark such as a navigational aid or small island, or in any terms which will assist a responding station in locating the vessel in distress. Include any information on vessel movement such as course, speed and destination.
Nature of distress (sinking, fire etc.).
Kind of assistance desired.
The number of persons onboard.
Any other information which might facilitate rescue, such as length or tonnage of the vessel, number of persons needing medical attention, color hull, cabin, masks, etc.
The word “OVER”

chapter_title: Sailing Basics: How To Use A Vhf Radio
text:
PAN: Boaters make this call when there is an urgent problem but it’s not life-threatening. You may hear this if a boater has lost engine power or is having navigational issues. The Coast Guard may follow up, but the boater is not necessarily requesting immediate help. As with Mayday, repeat PAN three times as in “PAN, PAN, PAN”.

SECURITY: (pronounced SAY-CURE-IT-TAY): A safety call, letting boaters in the area know about the movement of a large ship or other events. There is no danger, this is just for awareness. For example, in my local area, ferries will make a securite call when they’re going through a narrow pass between local islands or perhaps a navigational aid is drifting. Again, say it three times “SECURITY, SECURITY, SECURITY”.

chapter_title: Sailing Basics: How To Use A Vhf Radio
text:
A handful of useful VHF terms that are commonly used to keep conversations direct and brief, especially if you’re using channel 16.

THIS IS…  The main way to identify yourself, using the name of your boat. You use this after identifying the party you are calling (more on that in a moment).

OVER: Used when you’ve finished speaking and are expecting a reply.

ROGER: A quick way to say you understand what someone else is saying. “Roger” comes from the morse code days when “R” indicated “received”, and is sometimes understood as “Received Order Given, Expect Results.”

WILCO: “Wilco” means simply “will comply”. It’s often used with Roger as in “Roger Wilco” (message received, will comply).

REPLY: “Reply” is used to change channels, for example changing to a non-emergency or non-commercial channel if using channel 16. Usage is simply Reply + Channel#, as in “Reply 68” (i.e., reply on channel 68).

OUT: Used when you’ve finished speaking and a reply is not necessary.

*Pro tip: you should never use the phrase “over and out,” since the two words mean two opposite things!

SAY AGAIN:  Used when you need the speaker to repeat a portion or all of their previous transmission. This term is often used with:

ALL BEFORE…: Everything before whichever word you understood first.

ALL AFTER…: Everything after the word you last understood.

There are a couple of other rules to remember when it comes to lingo. You’ll want to learn the NATO phonetic alphabet. This is the standard way to clearly communicate single letters. When communicating numbers, you’ll want to communicate each number individually. For example, for the number 112, you would say, “One-one-two.”

“Heave to” with a little VHF language humor…

When using a VHF radio, three times is the charm
Whenever you use your radio to speak to another vessel, you should be addressing a particular party. Channel 16 not a broadcasting tool (unless you’re in distress, of course), and if you use channel 16 you must, must be brief!

There is a calling procedure that helps everyone listening to be clear on who is speaking, who is being addressed, and who needs to respond. Standard practice is to speak the name of the vessel (or marina) you’re addressing three times, then say “this is,” then the name of your boat. For example:

Lady Grey, Lady Grey, Lady Grey,

This is Time Out

Over

You would then wait for the other boat to respond. When responding to a message, you don’t need to say the vessel’s name three times again. So, for example, if the other vessel was to respond, they would say something like:

chapter_title: Securite, Mayday Repetition And Safety Escalation Sequences
section_titles: Responding To A SECURITE Message About A SAR Area
text: On hearing a SECURITE broadcast asking vessels to keep clear of a search-and-rescue area, note the position and extent of the area, plot it on the chart, and adjust the passage plan to stay well clear, typically at least two nautical miles unless the message states otherwise. Reduce speed, post an extra lookout, and if the new track will pass close regardless, call the station that issued the SECURITE to confirm safe passage: "MRCC, MRCC, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, REQUESTING CONFIRMATION SAFE TO PASS TWO MILES SOUTH OF THE REPORTED SAR AREA, OVER."

chapter_title: Securite, Mayday Repetition And Safety Escalation Sequences
section_titles: Diverting Course After A SECURITE Hazard Warning
text: On receiving a SECURITE warning about a hazard in your planned route, such as a drifting container, plot the hazard's reported position on the chart, calculate a safe passing distance of at least two nautical miles, plan the new course, and inform the crew before altering course. No special proword is needed to acknowledge a SECURITE broadcast unless a direct reply is required; the appropriate response is usually simply to act on the information and to log it.

section_titles: Repeating A MAYDAY Call After No Response
text: If no acknowledgement is heard within about fifteen seconds of a MAYDAY call, repeat the full MAYDAY call unchanged: "MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, THIS IS SEA OTTER, SEA OTTER, SEA OTTER, MAYDAY SEA OTTER, POSITION FIVE ZERO DECIMAL ONE TWO NORTH, ZERO ZERO ONE DECIMAL FOUR FIVE WEST, TAKING ON WATER, FOUR PERSONS ON BOARD, REQUIRE IMMEDIATE ASSISTANCE, OVER." If there is still no answer after several repeated attempts, some DSC sets automatically retransmit the DSC distress alert; the operator should also try switching to Channel 70 briefly to confirm the DSC alert itself was sent, then return to Channel 16 to keep repeating the voice MAYDAY.

section_titles: Repeating Essential Information On MRCC Request
text: When the MRCC (Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre) asks for a repeat of essential facts, respond promptly and slowly, digit by digit for anything numerical, and do not paraphrase: "THIS IS SEA OTTER, MY POSITION IS FIVE ZERO DEGREES ONE TWO DECIMAL FIVE MINUTES NORTH, ZERO ZERO ONE DEGREES FOUR FIVE DECIMAL THREE MINUTES WEST, PERSONS ON BOARD FIVE INCLUDING ONE INJURED, OVER."

chapter_title: Securite, Mayday Repetition And Safety Escalation Sequences
section_titles: Responding To A Request For Continuous Situation Updates
text:
When an MRCC requests continuous updates at defined intervals, acknowledge and follow a fixed schedule, for example every fifteen minutes on the working channel, and use a consistent structure each time: "MRCC, THIS IS SEA OTTER, UPDATE, POSITION FIVE ZERO DECIMAL ONE TWO NORTH ZERO ZERO ONE DECIMAL FOUR FIVE WEST, CONDITION NO CHANGE, NEXT UPDATE IN ONE FIVE MINUTES, OVER." If conditions worsen between scheduled updates, call immediately rather than waiting for the next scheduled slot.

A Full Escalation Sequence: Safety To Urgency To Medical Distress

A single developing situation can move through all three safety levels in sequence, and each stage needs its own correctly formatted call. First, a SECURITE warning is sent when a hazard is merely sighted: "SECURITE, SECURITE, SECURITE, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, HEAVY WEATHER DEVELOPING IN AREA, OUT." If the engine then fails and the vessel begins drifting seriously, this escalates to an urgency call: "PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, TOTAL LOSS OF PROPULSION, DRIFTING TOWARDS ROCKS, REQUESTING TOW, OVER." If a crew member is then injured and needs medical guidance, this becomes a PAN PAN MEDICO call, still using the PAN PAN urgency signal but specifically requesting medical advice rather than a general tow: "PAN PAN MEDICO, PAN PAN MEDICO, PAN PAN MEDICO, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, REQUESTING MEDICAL ADVICE FOR A CREW MEMBER WITH A SUSPECTED FRACTURE, OVER." If the vessel then genuinely starts taking on water and lives are in immediate danger, this escalates a final time to a full MAYDAY: "MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, TAKING ON WATER, FOUR PERSONS ON BOARD, REQUIRE IMMEDIATE ASSISTANCE, OVER." The key discipline is to always use the signal that matches the actual current severity of the situation, escalating (or de-escalating, once resolved) as conditions change, rather than jumping straight to MAYDAY for a situation that is not yet grave and imminent, or staying at a lower level once it genuinely becomes one.

When Not To Escalate Straight To MAYDAY

A vessel that is simply not under command, disabled, or requesting routine assistance is not automatically a MAYDAY situation; only grave and imminent danger to life justifies MAYDAY. For a vessel not under command but in no immediate danger, the correct call is a routine or, at most, a PAN PAN urgency call describing the situation and requesting assistance, not a distress call: "PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS SILENT WAVE, SILENT WAVE, SILENT WAVE, NOT UNDER COMMAND, DRIFTING, NO IMMEDIATE DANGER, REQUESTING A TOW, OVER." Sending an unwarranted MAYDAY diverts search-and-rescue resources from genuine emergencies and can result in the escalation being downgraded or disregarded by responding stations.

[Responding To A Request For Continuous Situation Updates — dialogue]
When an MRCC requests continuous updates at defined intervals, acknowledge and follow a fixed schedule, for example every fifteen minutes on the working channel, and use a consistent structure each time: "MRCC, THIS IS SEA OTTER, UPDATE, POSITION FIVE ZERO DECIMAL ONE TWO NORTH ZERO ZERO ONE DECIMAL FOUR FIVE WEST, CONDITION NO CHANGE, NEXT UPDATE IN ONE FIVE MINUTES, OVER." If conditions worsen between scheduled updates, call immediately rather than waiting for the next scheduled slot.

A Full Escalation Sequence: Safety To Urgency To Medical Distress

A single developing situation can move through all three safety levels in sequence, and each stage needs its own correctly formatted call. First, a SECURITE warning is sent when a hazard is merely sighted: "SECURITE, SECURITE, SECURITE, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, HEAVY WEATHER DEVELOPING IN AREA, OUT." If the engine then fails and the vessel begins drifting seriously, this escalates to an urgency call: "PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, TOTAL LOSS OF PROPULSION, DRIFTING TOWARDS ROCKS, REQUESTING TOW, OVER." If a crew member is then injured and needs medical guidance, this becomes a PAN PAN MEDICO call, still using the PAN PAN urgency signal but specifically requesting medical advice rather than a general tow: "PAN PAN MEDICO, PAN PAN MEDICO, PAN PAN MEDICO, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, REQUESTING MEDICAL ADVICE FOR A CREW MEMBER WITH A SUSPECTED FRACTURE, OVER." If the vessel then genuinely starts taking on water and lives are in immediate danger, this escalates a final time to a full MAYDAY: "MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, TAKING ON WATER, FOUR PERSONS ON BOARD, REQUIRE IMMEDIATE ASSISTANCE, OVER." The key discipline is to always use the signal that matches the actual current severity of the situation, escalating (or de-escalating, once resolved) as conditions change, rather than jumping straight to MAYDAY for a situation that is not yet grave and imminent, or staying at a lower level once it genuinely becomes one.

When Not To Escalate Straight To MAYDAY

A vessel that is simply not under command, disabled, or requesting routine assistance is not automatically a MAYDAY situation; only grave and imminent danger to life justifies MAYDAY. For a vessel not under command but in no immediate danger, the correct call is a routine or, at most, a PAN PAN urgency call describing the situation and requesting assistance, not a distress call: "PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS SILENT WAVE, SILENT WAVE, SILENT WAVE, NOT UNDER COMMAND, DRIFTING, NO IMMEDIATE DANGER, REQUESTING A TOW, OVER." Sending an unwarranted MAYDAY diverts search-and-rescue resources from genuine emergencies and can result in the escalation being downgraded or disregarded by responding stations.

chapter_title: Securite, Mayday Repetition And Safety Escalation Sequences
section_titles: De-Escalating Once A Situation Is Resolved
text: Once the original danger has passed, whichever level was declared should be formally cancelled so other stations stop diverting attention or resources to it. For a resolved urgency situation: "ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, PAN PAN CANCEL, ASSISTANCE NO LONGER REQUIRED, OUT." For a resolved distress situation, the same pattern is used with MAYDAY: "ALL STATIONS, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, MAYDAY CANCEL, VESSEL SAFE, NO FURTHER ASSISTANCE REQUIRED, OUT."

text: .A call sign is allocated to the vessel when first issued with a Ship Radio Licence. It uniquely identifies the vessel within the International Maritime Mobile Service. The call sign remains with the vessel for the duration of its life regardless of changes of ownership or even vessel name. However, the call sign is surrendered if the vessel ceases to be classed as a UK vessel, is destroyed or is unlicensed for a period of two or more years. Therefore every effort should be made to ensure that the call sign remains with the vessel. .Call signs cannot be transferred between vessels. .T-numbers (UK based call signs) are issued with Ship Portable Radio licences, as these radios are not intended for use on one vessel only.

[ — procedure]
.A call sign is allocated to the vessel when first issued with a Ship Radio Licence. It uniquely identifies the vessel within the International Maritime Mobile Service. The call sign remains with the vessel for the duration of its life regardless of changes of ownership or even vessel name. However, the call sign is surrendered if the vessel ceases to be classed as a UK vessel, is destroyed or is unlicensed for a period of two or more years. Therefore every effort should be made to ensure that the call sign remains with the vessel. .Call signs cannot be transferred between vessels. .T-numbers (UK based call signs) are issued with Ship Portable Radio licences, as these radios are not intended for use on one vessel only.

text: .A Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI) number uniquely identifies a vessel and is only issued to vessels fitted with Digital Selective Calling (DSC) and/or (Satellite) Ship Earth Station (SES) equipment. The UK administration does not normally issue MMSI numbers to EPIRBs/PLBs. .In order to use SES equipment, arrangements must be made with an Inmarsat Point of Service Activation Entity see Section  of these Guidance Notes. An MMSI number is required before the equipment can be commissioned. .If an MMSI has already been issued for use with DSC equipment and subsequentlyasatellite earth station terminal is installed, if a new MMSI is required, the DSC equipment may need to be re-programmed. MMSIs issued (as described above) arefree of charge as part of a Ship Radio Licence. .Ofcom notifies the ITU of all vessel MMSI numbers issued by the UK, however it does not notify Portable MMSI numbers. MMSIs are also made available to HM Coastguard to assist in Search and Rescue operations. .With the advent of VHF/DSC portable radios in  Ofcom has set aside a unique block of MMSI numbers which will be allocated only to this equipment. This enables HMCoastguardto differentiate between alerts sent from fixed and portable VHF/DSC radio equipment. However, such equipment is no longer being produced in the UK and consequently Ofcom onlyenvisages licensing equipment that is only currently on the market. .Portable VHF/DSC radios must on no account be programmed with the vessel MMSI numbers. .A Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI) number uniquely identifies a vessel and is only issued to vessels fitted with Digital Selective Calling (DSC) and/or (Satellite) Ship Earth Station (SES) equipment. text: Registration .A vessel does not need to be registered with an official body before an application for a Ship Radio licence is made. Under normal circumstances, Ofcom is not able to licence vessels registered in countries other than the UK, Isle of Man and Channel Islands. Vessels transferring away from the UK Flag to other Flag states must surrender their UK licence. .When a vessel needs to be registered to comply with the Merchant Shipping (Registration) Act , details may be obtained from The Registrar General, Maritime and Coastguard Agency. See Section  for contact details. .All changes to the Ship Radio licence or Ship Portable Radio licence details, e.g. change of owner’s address, radio equipment etc. must be notified to Ofcom in writing using the appropriate form Of . There is no charge for registering amendments. .The Ship Radio licencemust be kept with the radio equipment especially if the vessel is taken abroad. Foreign licensing administrations may confiscate the radio equipment or even detain the vessel, where a valid Ship Radio licencecannot be produced on demand. .Company applications – Whilst Ofcom is able to accept applications where a company is named as the licensee, a named contact must also be specified, and will be the first point of contact with Ofcom. If the company box is ticked, the applicant is declaring that the licensee is a limited company, and acompany registration number must be supplied. If the company is not a limited company then another appropriate box should be ticked.

text: .The ITU requires Ofcom to collect information about vessels being licensed and what equipment is being used. This information is held on the ITU’s Maritime Mobile Access and Retrieval System (MARS) database which is supplied for the use of Search and Rescue organisations worldwide. .Section  of the (application) form asks for information such as the gross tonnage of a vessel, its type and how many people it can carry. Ofcom is obliged to supply this information to the ITU and so if it is not completed in full on the application form Ofcom will be unable to issue a licence and the application form will be returned to the applicant. .Additional information which the ITU records on its MARS database is collected in Section  of the (application) form. This information is not mandatoryand a licencecan be issued even if it is not supplied. It is anticipated that much of this information is only relevant to larger passenger carrying vessels which routinely sail out of UK territorial waters. .The national telex number and Selcall number should be supplied where these have has been issued to the vessel. Please note that the Selcall system is becoming obsoleteand newnumbers should be requested onlyif needed. .Both the General Classification and Individual Classification fields are for codes that identify the type of vessel. A full list of these codes is given in Section  of these Guidance Notes. .The nature of service includes the classification as regards the type of international correspondence service maintained by the station, indicated bythe following codes: CO–a station open to official correspondence exclusively CP–a station open to public correspondence CR–a station open to limited public correspondence CV–a station open exclusively to correspondence of a private agency OT–a station open exclusively to operational traffic of the service concerned

text: Beacons (PLBs) are self contained battery operated radio transmitters, the purpose of which is tofacilitate search and rescue operations. EPIRBs and PLBs are intended for marine use only and should not be used on land. .There are several types of EPIRBs and PLBs in use in the United Kingdom; those that operate on the aeronautical distress frequencies . MHz or . MHz and  MHz and more sophisticated models operating on  MHz/. MHz and . GHz (these are becoming obsolete). These latter two have a unique identification code, which identifies the vessel to which it has been registered.

text: .The establishment and use of amateur radio stations on board United Kingdom licensed ships is permitted under the Amateur Radio Licence, granted byOfcom. On board a vessel, the licensee shall: a)install,use or makechanges tothe station only with the written permission of the vessel’s master; b)observeradio silence when required by the vessel’s master. .The full terms,provisions and limitations with which the licensee shall comply with are available from Ofcom. See Section . .It is important to ensure that radio is used correctly. At sea, lives may depend upon this. Consequently, there are severe penalties for not keeping within the law and these include fines, imprisonment and the forfeiture of anything used in connection with the offence. Those convicted of such offences may, in addition, face the revocation of their licence and the suspension of their Authority to operate.

text:
Mooring Marine is reader supported. When you buy through our links, we may get a commission.
You’ve got your new marine VHF radio connected and turned on. You hear the chatter from other boaters, and you… don’t exactly know what it all means. VHF Radio Lingo is quite confusing, but also pretty simple to decipher once you understand a few things.

In today’s article, we’re going to be taking a look at VHF radio lingo so that you’re able to properly communicate to other boaters and the Coast Guard should you ever run into trouble or just need to provide a standard status update.  You’ll learn everything you need to know to not sound silly if you need to use your radio!

text:
No products found.
VHF stands for Very High Frequency. It is the standard radio wave format used for marine communications. These types of waves function almost exactly like your standard FM radio waves and have a range of around 100 miles.

If you’re very close to shore, you’ll likely still have a cell phone signal or possibly Marine WiFi, especially if you use a Marine WiFi extender. But once you get out of range, a VHF Radio is critical for safety and communication.

This format makes them perfect for coastal transmissions, such as hailing a nearby boat or alerting the Coast Guard to your presence or predicament.

The reason VHF is used is that it’s particularly resistant to contamination such as atmospheric noise, rain, clouds, etc. The only thing that can really have a bad effect on VHF waves are electrical storms.

It’s also the main reason why VHF is not recommended for recreational vehicles to go out during severe weather. If they run into trouble, it can be a lot harder for them to get help.

Another reason that VHF is the most commonly used radio for boats is that it’s affordable. VHF radio technology is compact and most boating setups don’t cost more than a few hundred dollars, depending on the quality and brand.

This is perfect for the everyday boater.

text:
No products found.
One of the biggest mistakes that first-time boaters make is that they talk into their VHF radios like they were walkie talkies. This can cause a lot of confusion and misinterpretations. And that’s not something you want when you’re in need of emergency assistance!

If you’ve ever seen old military movies, then you’ve probably taken note of the times where the communication officer is on the old-school HAM radio using terms like “Alpha Whiskey Foxtrot, Over, Out, Copy” and more.

These are radio-specific terms that are designed to provide clarity and ease of communication so that there’s no confusion and parties can be easily understood.

It may seem a bit outdated with today’s technology, but keep in mind that these traditions developed out of military use so they’re probably not going anywhere anytime soon. Thankfully, they’re all fairly easy terms to remember and with a little bit of practice, you’ll be a pro in no time!

“Over” and “Out”
These are probably the two most common terms that most kids learn from watching TV and movies. A common mistake is for sailors to use both of these words in one sentence, saying “Over and Out.”

While it does have a nice ring to it, these two words each mean something different and should not be used together in the same phrase.

Over
Over is a statement that means you’ve completed your transmission (what you’re saying) and that you want a response from somebody on the other end. You’ll then take your finger off the transmit button and wait for a response.

Out
Out, on the other hand, means the exact opposite! Use this term to indicate that you’re finished with your transmission and you may not want a response back.

If you’re saying “over and out” and hoping for a response back, you may not get one! This is one of the most important radio terms for you and everybody on your boat to learn.

The phonetic alphabet is all standardized by NATO (The North Atlantic Trade Organization) and is recognized by all English-speaking countries and marine forces. Here’s a link if you want to see the full list. Do you best to memorize it, and keep a printed and laminated copy in your boat by the radio.

You don’t need to use the phonetic alphabet for every single word you say, but when it comes to important things (like the name of your ship, your personal name, etc.) these should always be used to provide clarity.

text: When you’re transmitting numbers, you should always say them in a digital format. For instance, instead of saying “twenty-two”, you should say “two-two”. This ensures that the numbers are clearly transmitted and there’s no confusion. Also, when saying the number nine, it’s common to use the term “niner” since nine is often confused for five.

[Transmitting Numbers — example]
When you’re transmitting numbers, you should always say them in a digital format. For instance, instead of saying “twenty-two”, you should say “two-two”. This ensures that the numbers are clearly transmitted and there’s no confusion. Also, when saying the number nine, it’s common to use the term “niner” since nine is often confused for five.

No products found.
If you’re trying to transmit the name of your boat, it’s a good idea to use call signs to help differentiate your boat from others. There may be multiple boats in the area with the same name as you.

If your boat is named The Dragon, it’s a good idea to use a custom call sign to differentiate your boat from other Dragons that might be on the same radio frequency. Instead, use a term like Whiskey-Dragon-Niner that’s unique and nobody else uses.

This is a good reason to come up with a good boat name. See our article on How to Name Your Boat for ideas.

How To Hail or Respond To Hails
If you want to hail another boat and you know its name, you should go to Channel 16 (the most common hailing frequency) and repeat the boat’s name three times followed by identifying your boat. E.g.- “Apollo, Apollo, Apollo, this is the ship Jupiter, do you read me?”

To respond, the other ship would say something like “I hear you loud and clear” indicating that the transmission was received clearly. After this, the two ships may switch to a different channel so that their conversation isn’t clogging up the hailing frequency for other boaters.

Last but not least, it’s important to understand emergency terms if the worst does happen.

The most common word that most people have heard is Mayday. This word lets other boaters and authorities know that you’re in a life-threatening situation and should only be used in deadly situations such as a sinking ship, deadly injury, running out of fuel and drifting away from shore, etc.

When making a Mayday call, always be sure to state your vessel’s name, how many crew members are on board, the problem that’s occurring, and your geographical position so that help can easily find you.

text: The radio spectrum worldwide is governed by the International Radio Regulations. In the UK the associated legislation is the Wireless Telegraphy (WT) Act 2006 (as amended). These regulations stipulate the licences that are required both for the radio installation and the radio operator. Although maritime (ship) radio’s primary function is to ensure safety of life at sea, the international radio regulations permit the use of ship radio on inland waterways as well as at sea. The rules for the installation and use of radio (e.g. VHF) apply equally when the equipment is used inland.

text: The Ship Portable Radio licence allows a named licensee to have one VHF portable maritime radio for use on different vessels, using a “T number” call sign.  (The radio must have an integral antenna and power supply).  Other radio equipment such as one EPIRB/PLB can also be included; further details are available at: http://www.ofcom.org.uk/radiocomms/ifi/licensing/classes/maritime /information/of168a.pdf The Ship Portable Radio Licence is intended for use in UK territorial waters only. Obtaining a Ship radio or Ship Portable Radio licence – online Since December 2006, using the Ofcom website, boat owners have been able to apply online free of charge for a new licence or to amend the details of an existing one.  Paper based applications are subject to a one off fee of £20. Although there is no end date on the licence, licensees must validate their licence at least once every ten years.  There is no charge for validating your licence, and it can be done either online or by using a paper based application form. There is no charge for amending (or validating licences), whether done on-line or by post. If a licensee sells their vessel it is important for them to surrender their licence.  This can be done online or by using a paper based form. Should they purchase a vessel they should apply for a new licence indicating the details of the vessel’s call sign and Maritime Mobile Service Identity where applicable, as these must remain with the vessel. It is still a legal requirement for vessel owners that have radio equipment with access to international channels on board their vessel, to have an up-to-date radio licence.  They must keep these on board where practicable and in any case must be kept on board www.rya.org.uk

[For safe and efficient shipping traffic in the Scheldt are — reference]
**For safe and efficient shipping traffic in the Scheldt area**

text:
These VHF procedures are a guideline for traffic controllers and traffic participants in the Scheldt area. Their aim is to clarify the use of VHF for safe and smooth shipping traffic. By correctly applying the procedures, other traffic participants will follow the good example, which will benefit safety.

The working procedures are based on the *IMO Guidelines For Vessel Traffic Services* (IMO Resolution A.1158(32)) and on the *IALA Guideline 1132 VTS Voice Communications and Phraseology*. In addition, various extra VHF regulations apply to specific vessel types, such as large gas tankers or oversized seagoing vessels. These regulations are not included in the general shipping procedures but are published via Joint Notices at www.vts-scheldt.net.

This document should be read together with the folder *VHF Sectors in the Scheldt Area*.

---

text:
**Duty to be reachable (Bereikbaarheidsplicht)**
Every vessel equipped with a VHF radio must always be reachable on the correct VHF channel, as stated in these procedures.

**Port information**
Information about bridges, berths and lock planning.

**Pilot advice under Pilotage from a Distance / Remote Pilotage (LOA)**
If a pilot cannot perform his or her duties on board the vessel being piloted, he or she may give advice remotely to a master and/or traffic participant. That advice may be given from another ship or from ashore (a traffic centre), under certain conditions.

**Overflow function**
The use of an additional VHF channel to relieve the regular traffic channel, for example to provide navigation assistance or to conduct other lengthy conversations.

**Radar channel**
This channel has an overflow function relative to the traffic channel. A radar channel is used to relieve the traffic channel, for example to provide navigation assistance or port information, or to conduct other conversations. Reachability on the traffic channel remains mandatory in the meantime.

**Traffic instruction (Verkeersaanwijzing)**
An order or prohibition imposed to bring about a specific result in traffic behaviour. The order or prohibition is imposed by an authorised person on one or more traffic participants.

**Traffic arrangement (Verkeersafspraak)**
An agreement made directly between traffic participants themselves, in order to prevent unclear situations and/or imminent danger. Traffic arrangements must be made directly between traffic participants and not via a traffic centre.

**Traffic centre**
The location from which a traffic controller carries out his or her duties. Within the GNB (Joint Nautical Management) there are five traffic centres.

**Traffic participant**
A participant who has actual control over the navigation of a vessel.

**General traffic information**
Information provided by a traffic controller relating to one or more traffic participants within the area of operation. The information may be intended to support the on-board navigational decision-making process, to monitor and plan vessels, or to respond to the development of unsafe situations.

**Traffic controller**
A certified person who, from a traffic centre, ensures the safe and smooth handling of shipping traffic.

**Mandatory reports**
Reports that traffic participants must make at prescribed points or times in order to keep shipping traffic safe and flowing smoothly.

**Area of operation**
The area of operation of the VHF procedures is indicated in the VHF Sectors document.

**Self-regulation**
Traffic participants may make traffic arrangements among themselves, without the intervention of a traffic centre. The traffic controller monitors the feasibility of the arrangements made.

section_titles: 2. Purpose of a Vessel Traffic Service
text:
A Vessel Traffic Service is a service implemented by the authorities that provides the means to communicate with shipping traffic and to respond to situations developing within the VTS area. The service increases the safety and efficiency of shipping and contributes to "Safety of Life at Sea" and to environmental protection.

A VTS is responsible for:

- **Providing timely and relevant information** about factors that may influence navigation and that support the on-board decision-making process.
  This includes, among other things, information on the position, identity and destination of other ships, and hydrological and meteorological information.

- **Monitoring and planning vessels** so as to contribute to the safe and smooth handling of shipping traffic.
  This involves providing essential, up-to-date and timely information to support the on-board navigational decision-making process. This support consists of providing timely information, advice and instructions. The information may relate to anything in the chain of operations, such as lock planning, tidal windows, the availability of pilotage services, and so on.

- **Providing timely and relevant information** to respond to the development of unsafe situations.
  Essential, up-to-date and timely information is provided to support the on-board navigational decision-making process. This support consists of providing timely information, advice and traffic instructions.

To achieve this, a VTS can provide information, warnings or traffic instructions where necessary.

text:
If users of VHF channels do not observe communication discipline, cross-talk occurs. This cross-talk, also known as interference, disrupts normal message traffic and creates questions that do not benefit safety. To prevent interference on the VHF channels, VHF users must observe the following rules:

- All conversations over VHF must be short, businesslike and clear, and take place on the correct channel (communication discipline).
- All VHF installations must transmit at a power of no more than 1 watt.
- Within VTS-SG, a reporting obligation and listening-watch obligation applies to all commercial shipping.
- For recreational craft with a VHF installation on board, a duty to be reachable applies, but not a reporting obligation (see the folder *VHF Sectors in the Scheldt Area*).
- Monitoring the traffic channel is mandatory at all times. In case of congestion or other circumstances, a radar channel can serve as an overflow.
- If a traffic controller foresees bottlenecks or dangerous situations, he or she actively intervenes to prevent problems. The traffic controller uses his or her authority to give a warning, information, advice or a traffic instruction.
- Without prejudice to the powers of the Flemish and Dutch authorities, and in the context of the safe and smooth handling of shipping traffic, ultimate responsibility for navigation always rests with the master/traffic participant.
- Traffic arrangements between ships, such as passing or overtaking not in accordance with the applicable navigation rules, are made directly between the ships themselves. When crossing, reference is usually made to the colour of the sidelights, for example: "We are passing green to green." When overtaking, reference is usually made to the side, for example: "I am passing on the port/starboard side." This is the traffic-regulating character of such arrangements.
- All traffic participants and traffic controllers must comply with these prescribed VHF procedures.

section_titles: 3.1 Communication discipline for VTS Scheldt Area participants
text:
- **Maintain communication discipline**, even if other participants do not.
- **Use the ship's name and the traffic centre's own name** in a call, not abbreviations or private names.
- Traffic participants with a reporting obligation **report in on the relevant channel**. Reporting off again is not necessary, unless a mandatory report applies.
- Traffic controllers ensure that **traffic participants make traffic arrangements among themselves** via the traffic channels. They may also mediate in this.
- **Do not hold discussions** on traffic channels.
- Use only the **approved working languages: Dutch or English**. In English, preferably use the Standard Marine Communication Phrases (SMCP). In an emergency, deviation from this is permitted.
- Use **message markers** (in both Dutch and English) to make clear the type of message.

In the management area of the GNA (Joint Nautical Authority), the Permanent Committee on Supervision of Scheldt Shipping has determined that the national language is also the working language in VHF communication. That is Dutch, with English as a fallback option (in accordance with SMCP).

text:
To promote communication discipline and to prevent overloading of the VHF channels in the VTS blocks, traffic controllers and all waterway users use the internationally established "message markers" to keep communication short, businesslike and clear.

These are the following eight indicators:

**MESSAGE MARKERS**

| Marker | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Information | Message contains observed facts |
| Question | Message has a questioning nature |
| Answer | Message is an answer to an earlier question |
| Intention | Message concerns intended navigational measures |
| Warning | Message is a warning of a potential danger |
| Request | Message asks the addressee(s) to take action |
| Advice | Sender wants to influence the addressee by means of a recommendation |
| Instruction | Sender wants to influence the addressee by means of a traffic instruction |

text:
The waterway user indicates when navigation assistance should be started and stopped by reporting in and out on the radar channel. The term **"navigation assistance"** is always used for this.¹

A traffic controller may also initiate the use of (elements of) navigation assistance on their own initiative in the event of deviant sailing behaviour.

- The traffic controller will confirm that the ship wants navigation assistance.
- In addition, the traffic controller will ask seagoing vessels in particular whether "buoy transits" (doorwisselen van boeien) are also desired.
  - Answer no: the traffic controller does not include the reporting of buoy transits as standard in the report.
  - Answer yes: the traffic controller includes the report of buoy transits (in a bend or during major course changes) as standard in the report.
- The waterway user then receives an initial message containing the following elements:
  - Understood/Acknowledged.
  - The own position of the ship that reported in for navigation assistance, according to the along/across method or the Bearing and Distance method (B/D method).
  - A relevant traffic picture of the ships in the vicinity.
- The traffic controller will also provide updates with the following content:
  - Own position of the ship according to the along/across or B/D method.
  - The aim is to provide this at least at every buoy or every second buoy, according to the traffic controller's assessment.
  - Update of the relevant² traffic picture, whereby work must also be done across block boundaries. Extra attention is given in this traffic picture to relevant overtaking manoeuvres and crossing traffic.
  - Any relevant passing distances, where applicable.
- Traffic arrangements must always be made on the traffic channel.

¹ No response is given to a request for assistance if reporting in is done using the terms "standing by" or "monitoring" on the radar channel.
² The information relevant to the traffic participant under navigation assistance (traffic, particulars, etc.) needed to form an up-to-date traffic picture in order to navigate smoothly, safely and efficiently.

text:
- Traffic participants must indicate in good time if they wish to deviate from a route.
- During navigation assistance, the traffic controller gives an overview of the current traffic picture, possibly supplemented with calculated, expected situations, such as encounters and passages in (passing) distance and time.
- To convey the position of a moving ship, the position of the bow of the vessel relative to a point ahead in the fairway, or in bearing and distance, is used. For a stationary ship, this is the middle of the track or a radar echo.
- The **passing distance** is the distance that will exist during passing between the adjacent sides of two ships, or between a ship and an obstacle. The passing distance is only reliable provided the ground track remains constant.
- The **ground track** of a ship is its direction of movement relative to true north over the ground.
- The **distance between two vessels** is the measured shortest distance. For head-on traffic this is the bow-to-bow distance; for overtaking traffic this is the bow-to-stern distance.
- The **abeam distance** to a buoy, beacon or obstacle is the distance between the bow of a moving ship and an object, measured perpendicular to the direction of the fairway.
- The **distance to a navigation mark** is the shortest distance to that navigation mark.
- The terms **"opvarend" (upbound)** and **"afvarend" (downbound)** are used east of the Schone Waardin. In English these are "ingoing" and "outgoing".
- In the approach areas and the roadstead area, the terms **"inkomend" (inbound)** and **"uitgaand" (outbound)** are used, in English "inbound" and "outbound".
- To indicate a position before or beyond a certain point, we use **"bovenwaarts" (upstream)** or **"benedenwaarts" (downstream)**. In English these are "above" and "below".
- If the traffic controller must give information about a part of the area not covered by radar and for which no visual information is available, he or she will make this known to the traffic participant requesting the information.
- Position information is always given relative to known reference points. These points are visible, known and can be found on the nautical chart.
- A **bearing** between two known points is the horizontal angle relative to true north and the point being observed. The figures are spoken one by one.
- **Distances** are given to a tenth of a kilometre or a tenth of a nautical mile (also called a "cable"). Where confusion is possible, e.g. between the English numbers fifty and fifteen, the digits are spoken separately.
- Names of buoys and markers must not be translated. They are pronounced as they appear on the nautical chart. For example, W6 is pronounced "Whiskey 6".
- "Buoy transit" (doorwisselen van boeien) refers to two consecutive buoys marking a bend in a channel coming into line relative to the bow of the ship.
- Position reports can be given in two ways: using the along/across method, or via bearing and distance. The traffic controller may supplement this with ground track and ground speed. The intervals between reports depend on the traffic picture, the speeds of vessels, meteorological conditions, nautically critical points, and so on.
- An **along/across position report** comprises, on the one hand, the point to which the ship has progressed along the length of the fairway, and on the other hand, the distance of the ship in the transverse direction, measured to the locally customary reference line — for example the buoy line, the light line, the shore, etc. The transverse distance may also be expressed as 1/3 red, 1/3 green, or mid-channel. If the distance is less than 1/3 of the fairway width, the distance is expressed in metres to the buoy line.
  Measurements are always given relative to the starboard side (SB) of the vessel. If this is not possible because there is no reference, the traffic controller will explicitly state this.
- A **position report via bearing and distance** looks at the position of the forward part of the assisted ship in relation to a known point.
  Here too, the traffic controller may add ground track and ground speed. If the ship is sailing parallel to the reference line, moving away from it, or approaching it, this will be stated.
- If the traffic controller gives position reports (on request) while a ship is coming to anchor, he or she agrees which point the reports will be relative to. Either the planned anchor position is indicated — this may be an anchorage as shown on the chart, or a position chosen by the master or pilot. From the bow, the traffic controller gives information by bearing and distance (B/D) to the anchor position, including speed over ground. As a standard for reporting frequency, the following applies:
  - Distance more than 1500 m: B/D every 500 m
  - Distance 1500 to 500 m: B/D every 200 m
  - Distance 500 to 200 m: B/D every 100 m
  - From 200 m: B/D every 50 m.

For anchor watch purposes, the master or pilot must state the number of nautical miles and/or cables relative to a fixed point, and the number of shackles on deck.

text_with_context:
Source: VHF-procedures-Scheldt-area-EN.md  ·  Chapter: VHF PROCEDURES

[Explanation — dialogue]
- Traffic participants must indicate in good time if they wish to deviate from a route.
- During navigation assistance, the traffic controller gives an overview of the current traffic picture, possibly supplemented with calculated, expected situations, such as encounters and passages in (passing) distance and time.
- To convey the position of a moving ship, the position of the bow of the vessel relative to a point ahead in the fairway, or in bearing and distance, is used. For a stationary ship, this is the middle of the track or a radar echo.
- The **passing distance** is the distance that will exist during passing between the adjacent sides of two ships, or between a ship and an obstacle. The passing distance is only reliable provided the ground track remains constant.
- The **ground track** of a ship is its direction of movement relative to true north over the ground.
- The **distance between two vessels** is the measured shortest distance. For head-on traffic this is the bow-to-bow distance; for overtaking traffic this is the bow-to-stern distance.
- The **abeam distance** to a buoy, beacon or obstacle is the distance between the bow of a moving ship and an object, measured perpendicular to the direction of the fairway.
- The **distance to a navigation mark** is the shortest distance to that navigation mark.
- The terms **"opvarend" (upbound)** and **"afvarend" (downbound)** are used east of the Schone Waardin. In English these are "ingoing" and "outgoing".
- In the approach areas and the roadstead area, the terms **"inkomend" (inbound)** and **"uitgaand" (outbound)** are used, in English "inbound" and "outbound".
- To indicate a position before or beyond a certain point, we use **"bovenwaarts" (upstream)** or **"benedenwaarts" (downstream)**. In English these are "above" and "below".
- If the traffic controller must give information about a part of the area not covered by radar and for which no visual information is available, he or she will make this known to the traffic participant requesting the information.
- Position information is always given relative to known reference points. These points are visible, known and can be found on the nautical chart.
- A **bearing** between two known points is the horizontal angle relative to true north and the point being observed. The figures are spoken one by one.
- **Distances** are given to a tenth of a kilometre or a tenth of a nautical mile (also called a "cable"). Where confusion is possible, e.g. between the English numbers fifty and fifteen, the digits are spoken separately.
- Names of buoys and markers must not be translated. They are pronounced as they appear on the nautical chart. For example, W6 is pronounced "Whiskey 6".
- "Buoy transit" (doorwisselen van boeien) refers to two consecutive buoys marking a bend in a channel coming into line relative to the bow of the ship.
- Position reports can be given in two ways: using the along/across method, or via bearing and distance. The traffic controller may supplement this with ground track and ground speed. The intervals between reports depend on the traffic picture, the speeds of vessels, meteorological conditions, nautically critical points, and so on.
- An **along/across position report** comprises, on the one hand, the point to which the ship has progressed along the length of the fairway, and on the other hand, the distance of the ship in the transverse direction, measured to the locally customary reference line — for example the buoy line, the light line, the shore, etc. The transverse distance may also be expressed as 1/3 red, 1/3 green, or mid-channel. If the distance is less than 1/3 of the fairway width, the distance is expressed in metres to the buoy line.
  Measurements are always given relative to the starboard side (SB) of the vessel. If this is not possible because there is no reference, the traffic controller will explicitly state this.
- A **position report via bearing and distance** looks at the position of the forward part of the assisted ship in relation to a known point.
  Here too, the traffic controller may add ground track and ground speed. If the ship is sailing parallel to the reference line, moving away from it, or approaching it, this will be stated.
- If the traffic controller gives position reports (on request) while a ship is coming to anchor, he or she agrees which point the reports will be relative to. Either the planned anchor position is indicated — this may be an anchorage as shown on the chart, or a position chosen by the master or pilot. From the bow, the traffic controller gives information by bearing and distance (B/D) to the anchor position, including speed over ground. As a standard for reporting frequency, the following applies:
  - Distance more than 1500 m: B/D every 500 m
  - Distance 1500 to 500 m: B/D every 200 m
  - Distance 500 to 200 m: B/D every 100 m
  - From 200 m: B/D every 50 m.

For anchor watch purposes, the master or pilot must state the number of nautical miles and/or cables relative to a fixed point, and the number of shackles on deck.

section_titles: 10.2 Area description, VHF channels and times
text:
The Scheldt Shipping Report (SSB) aims to provide information of a general nature to waterway users. The content of the SSB includes:

- Water levels and expected deviations at various measuring points in the area
- Expected cross-current reports off buoy 53
- Wind direction and strength at the traffic centre, storm warnings, local wind forecasts
- Visibility reports (where applicable)
- Shipping traffic, particulars and important works
- Significant deviations in fairway marking
- Depending on the traffic centre: pilotage information such as the side of the pilot ladder, storm pilotage, significant wave height at Kwintebank (GHs KWI) from 2.0 metres, and so on
- For Zeebrugge Traffic Centre only: traffic pictures within the area of operation concerning ships with a draught of ≥140 dm, or ships which, due to their tidal window (GNA), cannot deviate

[SECTION BREAK]

Four area-specific Scheldt Shipping Reports are broadcast. These are broadcast at different times so that they do not overlap.

Page 5 of 22 Introduction My first introduction to a VHF radio was while enjoying a weeklong sailing vacation around the Greek Ionian Islands. My husband, Simon, and I joined forces with another couple and hired a 33’ sailboat. The four of us became part of a sailing flotilla. Every morning, we would be briefed on our destination for the day. The vacation coordinators would ensure we left our mooring and help us dock up later in the afternoon. We had to use the VHF radio to communicate with the coordinators or ‘Lead Boat Crew,’ who kept close by. Thankfully, my husband and one of our friends handled all the communications, as my girlfriend and I were too scared to use the radio. I’m unsure what caused my fear of the radio – perhaps I didn’t want to make a mistake? Our initial sailing vacation ended up being a huge success. My husband and I were hooked for life. We enjoyed ten more years of sailing excursions and eventually purchased our first boat – a Moody 35’ sailboat. In the UK, where we kept our Moody, the maritime law requires that at least one person per boat possesses a Marine Radio Short Range Certificate (SRC). The SRC, which must be completed at a recognized training center, instructs users in radio etiquette and procedures, digital selected calling (DSC), and emergency procedures. Simon took the full-day course, passed the exam, and was granted a license. Fortunately for me, I once again dodged responsibility for the VHF radio. Side note: I have good news for you if you're in the US. The Telecommunications Act of 1996 permits recreational boaters to have and use a VHF marine radio, EPIRB, and marine radar without having an FCC ship station license. So, if you’re in the US, you don’t need a license; however, that doesn’t mean you shouldn’t learn how to use the VHF. VHF knowledge could mean the difference between life and death. Keep reading!
