Eventually, we traded our 35’ Moody for a 56’ Oyster sailboat, sold all our possessions, and decided to sail worldwide. At that point, I thought the time had come to face my fear of the VHF finally. But did I need to really take a course on the radio?

section_titles: Is a VHF radio course essential to take?
text: After sailing around the Solent, a massively busy waterway off England’s south coast, and listening to the VHF radio for a couple of years, I initially pooh-poohed the idea of getting my VHF License. Simon took the VHF radio course and obtained a license when we first purchased our boat, so as long as one person had a license, I felt OK to let him hold all the knowledge. And frankly, I always thought, ‘How hard can it be?’ I could quickly call up the marina and ask for a berth if I had to, so anything else would be similar. Yes? And if the worst-case scenario happened, and I had to make a MAYDAY call, I would push the scary red button on the radio and then follow the template taped to the underside of our navigation table left by the previous owner. What if… However, deciding to sell up and sail worldwide made me think twice about my VHF radio knowledge. If I did have to do a MAYDAY, would I do it correctly, considering the panic situation I’d most likely be in? Would I know how to figure out where I am? What if Simon wasn’t around and I received a DSC (Digital Selective Calling) alert – would I know how to respond? What is a DSC alert anyway? And what if our young daughter accidentally triggered the red button on the radio that is labeled ‘Distress’? Visit SailingBritican.com to become a confident sailing cruiser! Page 7 of 22

section_titles: The most important thing about sailing is safety
text: The most important thing about sailing is safety. If our boat is going to go down, my husband, crew, and I need to know exactly what to do. Furthermore, if someone else is in our vicinity and we can help to save lives, again, we need to know what to do. Hubby booked me on the VHF radio course. The pain of not knowing or having confidence in using the VHF radio became uncomfortable. Simon booked me on a VHF radio course in Southampton, England. Steve Gravells from Technical Recreational Coaching led a class of nine of us. Steve sent us the Royal Yachting Association (RYA) VHF radio course booklet a couple of weeks before the course, so we didn’t have to spend time learning the information from the book. If it weren’t for the homework that Steve requested before our class – a page of questions to be filled out – I would have failed to read the book. Again – I thought, ‘How hard can this be?’ Knowing I had homework to do, I read the book and did the homework. The RYA VHF radio booklet was beneficial. Aside from the first couple of pages filled with acronyms (R&TTE, DSC, SRC, CEPT) that I knew I would never remember, the RYA book was straightforward and easy to read. It took 30 minutes to get through, and I was full of information when I finished. Poor Simon had to listen to me say, “Did you know the word MAYDAY comes from the French word, M’aidez, and it means ‘help me’? And did you know that you need to send out a DSC (Digital Selective Calling) Alert before making a Pan-Pan voice broadcast?”

section_titles: Arriving at the Southampton Dry Stack after eating…
text: Arriving at the Southampton Dry Stack after eating a bacon roll, I was eager to put the day behind me. I’ve never been a fan of courses. I get bored quickly, and I wouldn’t say I like a numb bum – the sensation you get when sitting too long. Well, I was pleasantly surprised with the flow of the course. Never during the day did I wish that time would pass quickly. There was a mix of learning, watching, using the radio, coffee breaks, and general socializing. Everything taught was practical – it wasn’t theory or something that would go in one ear and out the other. And it was so powerful to see the difference between learning how to use the radio and then using it. Most of us seemed like we had it mastered, but when we went to (pretend) call another boat, the Coastguard, or make a MAYDAY, we found it more complicated than we thought. Ensuring to say who you are and whom you’re calling and finishing the message with the correct ‘over’ or ‘out’ wasn’t as easy as it looked! And talking slowly enough for others to write your MAYDAY was challenging. Not one person in the class spoke slowly enough for the other members to correctly note all the MAYDAY information. Thankfully, by the end of the day, the whole class sounded much better than when we started. That’s because Steve would have us go through the call if we didn’t get it right. To say that just my confidence increased would be an understatement. My faith, knowledge, and the importance of the subject matter increased. Learning how to use the VHF radio is not about making sure you can call a marina to request a berth – it’s a device to potentially save your life and the lives of those in your area. Until I took the course, I didn’t realize that the alarm that periodically went off on my boat was an urgent message alert. section_titles: So, is a VHF radio course necessary to take?
text: My answer is a definite ‘Yes.’ Unfortunately, it’s one of those situations where you don’t know what you don’t know. By taking the course, you’ll increase your confidence in using a VHF radio, understand how to maneuver your way around the menu system, and, most importantly, understand what to do when an emergency strikes. Overall, the VHF radio course is invaluable, and everyone in the boating community should take the course. Whether you take a VHF course or not, it is very easy to forget how to instigate a DSC distress or urgency message and follow up with the correct broadcast message. Furthermore, remaining calm in a potentially life-threatening situation or emergency can be challenging. By having quick, easy-to-understand, accessible instructions and broadcast templates, you make it easier for yourself to broadcast correctly and have a system that allows others who might not know how to use the VHF but are forced to do so. Within this guide, you’ll discover an explanation and an example of the various VHF calls, followed up with checklist templates ready for use. Furthermore, I’ve added various information, tips, and personal experiences to help make using the VHF radio easier. Taking a class is great, but if that’s not going to happen, this guide will provide you with everything you need to know to be a confident sailing cruiser. chapter_title: What is a VHF Radio, and why is it Important?
text: A VHF radio is a two-way radio system that operates in the VHF frequency range, typically between 156.0 and 174.0 MHz. It is commonly used in the maritime industry and among sailors for emergency and routine communication. VHF radios are compact, easy to use, and designed to transmit and receive voice messages over relatively short to medium distances, making them ideal for maritime communication.

section_titles: Emergency Communication: VHF radios are a primary tool for emergency
text: communication on the water. Channel 16, often called the "distress channel," is dedicated to emergency calls. Sailors can use VHF radios to transmit distress signals (MAYDAY calls) when facing life-threatening situations, such as sinking, medical emergencies, or man-overboard incidents. Reliable Coverage: VHF radio signals have excellent coverage in coastal and open water areas, providing sailors with reliable communication even when far from shore. This makes VHF radios especially valuable for offshore sailing and long-distance cruising.

As you embark on your sailing adventure, one of the essential skills you’ll need to master is the proper use of VHF (Very High Frequency) radio. This communication tool is vital for ensuring the safety of your vessel and crew, as well as maintaining good relations with fellow sailors and the maritime community. section_titles: VHF Radio Etiquette Do’s and Don’ts
text:
Why VHF Radio is Important
VHF radio is a crucial tool for sailors, as it allows for communication with other vessels, marinas, and emergency services. It is essential for coordinating with other boats, receiving weather updates, and calling for assistance in case of an emergency. Additionally, proper use of VHF radio can help prevent accidents and misunderstandings, ensuring a safe and enjoyable sailing experience for all.

section_titles: VHF Radio Channels and Their Uses
text:
VHF radios operate on a range of channels, each designated for specific purposes. Here are some of the most commonly used channels and their functions:

Channel 16: This is the international distress, safety, and calling channel. It is used for making initial contact with other vessels or shore stations and for emergency communications. Once contact is established, you should switch to a working channel to continue your conversation.
Channel 13: This channel is used for bridge-to-bridge communication between vessels, primarily for navigational purposes.
Channel 9: In some areas, this channel is designated as an alternate calling channel for non-commercial vessels.
Channels 68, 69, 71, 72, and 78A: These are common working channels for recreational boaters. Once you have established contact on channel 16, you can switch to one of these channels for your conversation.
It’s essential to familiarize yourself with the specific channel assignments in your sailing area, as they may vary by region. Consult your VHF radio’s manual or local maritime authorities for more information.

text:
To ensure clear and effective communication, it’s essential to follow proper VHF radio procedures. Here are the basic steps for initiating and conducting a VHF radio conversation:

Listen before transmitting: Before you begin speaking, listen to the channel to ensure it is not currently in use.
Select the appropriate channel: Choose the correct channel for your intended communication, as outlined in the previous section.
Press the transmit button: Hold the microphone about 2 inches from your mouth, press the transmit button, and wait for a second before speaking to ensure your transmission is not cut off.
State your call sign or vessel name: Begin your transmission by stating your vessel’s name or call sign, followed by the name or call sign of the vessel or station you are trying to contact. Repeat this process three times for initial contact.
Switch to a working channel: Once contact is established, agree on a working channel and switch to that channel to continue your conversation.
End your transmission: When you have finished speaking, release the transmit button and wait for a response. To conclude your conversation, state your vessel’s name or call sign and the word “out.”

section_titles: Tips for Clear and Effective Communication
text:
To ensure clear and concise communication, it’s essential to use standard VHF radio phrases. Here are some common terms and their meanings:

Over: This indicates that you have finished speaking and are waiting for a response.
Out: This signifies the end of your conversation. No response is expected.
Roger: This means that you have received and understood the message.
Affirmative: This is used to indicate agreement or confirmation.
Negative: This is used to indicate disagreement or refusal.
Standby: This means that you are temporarily unable to respond or need a moment to gather information. The other party should wait for your response.
Mayday: This is the international distress signal, used only in life-threatening emergencies.
Pan-Pan: This is the international urgency signal, used for situations that are not immediately life-threatening but require assistance.
Securité: This is the international safety signal, used to broadcast important safety information or navigational warnings.

[SECTION BREAK]

To ensure your VHF radio transmissions are easily understood, follow these tips for clear and effective communication:

Speak slowly and clearly, enunciating each word.
Use plain language whenever possible, avoiding slang or jargon.
Repeat important information, such as numbers or coordinates, for clarity.
Spell out words using the phonetic alphabet (e.g., Alpha, Bravo, Charlie) if there is any potential for confusion.
Keep your transmissions brief and to the point, avoiding unnecessary chatter.

section_titles: VHF Radio Etiquette Do’s and Don’ts
text:
To maintain good relations with fellow sailors and the maritime community, it’s essential to follow proper VHF radio etiquette. Here are some do’s and don’ts to keep in mind:

Do:

Monitor channel 16 when not actively using your VHF radio, in case of emergency calls or important announcements.
Use the lowest power setting necessary to communicate effectively, to minimize interference with other vessels.
Be patient and courteous when communicating with other vessels or shore stations, even if they are not following proper procedures.
Don’t:

Use profanity or offensive language, as VHF radio transmissions can be heard by anyone monitoring the channel.
Engage in unnecessary chatter or lengthy conversations, as this can tie up the channel and prevent others from using it.
Transmit false distress or emergency calls, as this is illegal and can result in severe penalties.
By following these guidelines and mastering the art of VHF radio etiquette, you’ll be well-equipped to communicate effectively and safely with fellow sailors and maritime authorities. This essential skill will not only enhance your sailing experience but also contribute to the safety and enjoyment of all those who share the open sea.

text: The VHF antenna cable is a low-loss coaxial cable, typically RG-8X for shorter runs or RG-213 or LMR-400 for longer masthead runs, terminated with a PL-259 connector at the radio end and a matching connector at the antenna base. It carries the transmitted RF energy from the radio to the antenna and the received signal back down; a damaged, corroded, or poorly seated connector increases signal loss and can drastically reduce both transmit range and receive sensitivity even if the radio itself is working perfectly. The connector should be kept dry, greased with dielectric grease where exposed to weather, and checked periodically for a tight, corrosion-free fit.

chapter_title: Vhf Radio Hardware, Installation And Handheld Care
section_titles: Cleaning Contacts And Seals On A Handheld Unit
text:
Power the unit off and remove the battery pack before cleaning. Wipe the metal battery-pack contacts and the corresponding contacts inside the radio body with a soft, dry cloth, or a cotton bud very lightly moistened with isopropyl alcohol; never use an abrasive material, which can scratch the contact plating and cause poor conduction later. Inspect the rubber gasket or O-ring seals around the battery compartment and any port flaps for grit, cracking, or compression damage, and gently clean them with a dry, soft brush, since a compromised seal is the most common cause of water ingress in an otherwise waterproof handheld.

[SECTION BREAK]

Use only the charger supplied by, or explicitly approved by, the radio's manufacturer, since a mismatched charger's voltage or current can damage the battery or, in rare cases, create a fire risk. Charge in a dry, ventilated location, and avoid leaving a fully charged battery on trickle charge indefinitely for extended periods if the manufacturer's manual recommends periodic full discharge cycles to preserve battery capacity.

chapter_title: Vhf Radio Hardware, Installation And Handheld Care
section_titles: Checking The VSWR (Voltage Standing Wave Ratio) Of An Installation
text: A high VSWR reading indicates a poor match between the radio, the cable, and the antenna, usually caused by a damaged cable, a corroded connector, or an incorrectly tuned or damaged antenna, and it both reduces transmitted range and can, at extreme levels, damage the radio's output transistor over time. A basic in-line VSWR meter, inserted between the radio and the antenna cable, should read low (typically below about 1.5:1) on a healthy installation; a high or rapidly rising reading is a sign to inspect the cable run and connectors before the set is used for anything safety-critical.

chapter_title: Vhf Radio Hardware, Installation And Handheld Care
section_titles: Choosing A Mounting Location For A Fixed-Mount Radio
text:
A fixed-mount VHF set should be mounted where it is reachable from the helm without leaving the wheel, protected from direct spray and sun, and with enough clearance behind the panel for the power and antenna cables to be connected without being sharply bent. Keeping the set close to the main power source reduces voltage drop in the supply cable, which can otherwise cause the radio to reset or transmit at reduced power during heavy current draw.

[SECTION BREAK]

A fixed VHF radio should be wired with an appropriately rated fuse close to the power source, not just at the radio end, and with cable heavy enough to avoid significant voltage drop over the length of the run; undersized power cable is a common, easily overlooked cause of a radio that transmits weakly or resets under load even though the antenna and cable to the antenna are both healthy.

chapter_title: Spelling Practice For Vhf Radio Communication
section_titles: Spelling out a word correctly on VHF radio is a core operato
text: Spelling out a word correctly on VHF radio is a core operator skill, required whenever a vessel name, a person's surname, a place name, or a technical term could be misheard due to static, weak signal, or similarly-sounding letters. Before spelling, the operator says "I SPELL" so the listening station knows individual letters follow rather than a normal word, then gives each letter using its NATO phonetic code word, and finally says "I SPELL" again followed by "OVER" to indicate the spelling is complete and hand the transmission back. The listening station should then read the spelled word back to confirm it was understood correctly. The examples below cover a wide range of realistic situations an operator will encounter: vessel names, surnames, given names, place names, waypoint and buoy names, cargo and technical terms, company and callsign fragments, harbor and port names, weather and position terms, and radio equipment terms.

section_titles: Background sources cited in PLA Safety Bulletin SB3-25, "Proper Use of VHF
text:
This document summarizes, in plain language, each of the nine sources listed in the "Further Reading" table of the Port of London Authority's Safety Bulletin SB3-25. These are the international, EU-derived, and UK legal and guidance instruments that together set out how VHF marine radio must be used. Each summary is written independently of the source text and is not a substitute for reading the original — links are provided at the end of each section.

---

text:
**Source:** International Maritime Organization (IMO), International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, 1974, Chapter IV
**Link:** https://www.imo.org/en/About/Conventions/Pages/International-Convention-for-the-Safety-of-Life-at-Sea-(SOLAS),-1974.aspx

SOLAS is the core international treaty governing ship safety, and Chapter IV of its Annex deals specifically with radiocommunications. Its purpose is to guarantee that ships covered by the Convention are equipped so they can reliably send and receive distress and safety information, coordinate with each other and with shore authorities in emergencies, and call on organized search-and-rescue services when needed. The chapter also ensures that radio installations across different vessels and shore stations are technically compatible with one another, that they remain functional even after a single equipment failure (i.e., there is built-in redundancy), and that they are properly maintained throughout a ship's operational life.

Chapter IV applies to all passenger ships on international voyages and to cargo ships of 300 gross tonnage or more on international voyages. It underpins the Global Maritime Distress and Safety System (GMDSS), the internationally standardized system of satellite and terrestrial communication procedures used for maritime distress alerting.

The chapter has been substantially revised over time to keep pace with changing technology. A major modernization came into force on 1 January 2024 (via IMO Resolution MSC.496(105)), which updated the GMDSS to reflect the shift away from older systems. Under the revised chapter, ships operating in certain sea areas (A3/A4) are no longer required to carry high-frequency narrow-band direct-printing telegraphy (HF NBDP) equipment for transmitting and receiving distress and safety messages, and NAVTEX/EGC/HF NBDP receivers are no longer automatically mandatory — although owners may retain such equipment voluntarily for receiving maritime safety information. The amendments also broadened recognition of satellite service providers beyond Inmarsat to include other "Recognized Mobile Satellite Service" providers, such as Iridium, where a flag state accepts them.

In UK law, SOLAS Chapter IV's requirements are given direct legal effect through the Merchant Shipping (Radiocommunications) (Amendment) Regulations 2021 (see Section 2 below), and MCA Marine Guidance Note 641 (M) explains how UK-flagged ships and operators should apply it in practice.

---

section_titles: Source:** UK Statutory Instrument, in force from 24 December 2021
text:
**Link:** https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2021/1316/contents/made

This Statutory Instrument is how the UK brings SOLAS Chapter IV into domestic law. It has two main effects. First, it directly imposes the SOLAS Chapter IV radiocommunications requirements on UK ships (and non-UK ships in UK waters) undertaking international voyages. Second, it amends the earlier Merchant Shipping (Radio Installations) Regulations 1998 so that ships on non-international voyages continue to have appropriate radio requirements, while ships covered by the Convention now only need to comply with the 2021 Regulations rather than the 1998 ones.

Structurally, the Regulations are organized into four parts. Part 1 covers general matters: citation and commencement, definitions, which ships the rules apply to, and provisions allowing the Secretary of State to grant exemptions or approve equivalent arrangements where full compliance would be unreasonable or impractical for a particular vessel. Part 2 sets out the basic functional requirement that ships must be able to transmit and receive distress and safety communications. Part 3 deals with the technical detail: performance standards for equipment, requirements for radio installations, watchkeeping obligations, maintenance duties, qualifications for radio personnel, record-keeping, and equipment testing. Part 4 covers enforcement — offences, penalties, and a ship's potential detention if it fails to comply.

A distinctive and important feature of these Regulations is the "ambulatory reference" provision (regulation 7). This means that whenever SOLAS Chapter IV is amended internationally in future, those changes are automatically incorporated into UK law at the same time, without needing a fresh Statutory Instrument each time. This keeps UK requirements permanently aligned with the current international standard.

The Regulations apply, with limited exceptions, to United Kingdom ships wherever they are, and to non-UK ships (including those from countries that haven't ratified SOLAS) while they are in UK waters.

text:
**Link:** https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/mgn-641-amendment-1-m-guidance-on-radiocommunications-under-chapter-iv-of-solas

MGN 641 (M) is the MCA's practical guidance document explaining how shipowners, masters, shipbuilders, and seafarers should interpret and apply the Merchant Shipping (Radiocommunications) (Amendment) Regulations 2021 described above. Rather than creating new legal obligations itself, it is meant to be read alongside the 2021 Regulations to clarify what compliance looks like in practice — and in fact parts of the Note have been given the force of law by the Regulations.

The guidance is structured around eight key topic areas: an introduction to the legal framework; how "recognised satellite service providers" are determined; requirements for radio installation on board; the sources of electrical energy that must be available to power radio equipment (including backup power in case of failure); the performance standards equipment must meet; maintenance requirements to keep radio equipment serviceable; qualifications and duties required of radio personnel on board; and the record-keeping obligations for radio logs.

Because the Regulations incorporate future SOLAS amendments automatically via the ambulatory reference mechanism, the guidance note is periodically reissued or amended (there have been at least one or two amendments since first publication in December 2021) to reflect the latest position and remove ambiguity for those applying the rules day to day.

text:
**Source:** UK Public General Act, 2006 c. 36, Parliament of the United Kingdom
**Link:** https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/36/contents

The Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006 is the principal UK statute governing the use of radio apparatus of all kinds — not just maritime — including marine VHF sets. It received Royal Assent on 8 November 2006 and largely consolidated earlier wireless telegraphy legislation (including the Wireless Telegraphy Acts of 1949 and 1967) into a single, modernized Act, while also repealing a range of older enactments. It applies across the whole of the United Kingdom.

The Act gives Ofcom its general statutory functions over the radio spectrum, including licensing radio apparatus and enforcing compliance. Two aspects of the Act are directly relevant to the misuse of VHF radio referenced in the PLA bulletin. Section 48 makes it a criminal offence to use wireless telegraphy apparatus to intentionally intercept the contents of a message not intended for the interceptor, or to disclose the contents, sender, or addressee of such a message obtained that way — a provision aimed at protecting the privacy and integrity of radio communications, including on marine VHF channels. Section 116 defines "wireless telegraphy" broadly, in essence covering the transmission or reception of electromagnetic energy up to 3,000 gigahertz used for conveying messages, sounds, or images, or for operating equipment, or for determining position or detecting objects — a definition wide enough to capture VHF, radar, and AIS.

More broadly, operating radio apparatus without the required licence, or in a way inconsistent with licence conditions, is an offence under the Act, and this is the legal basis referenced by the PLA bulletin when it warns that "unnecessary transmission" or "non-standard phrases" on VHF may constitute a breach of the Act. The Act has been amended numerous times since 2006 (for example by the Digital Economy Acts of 2010 and 2017, and the Investigatory Powers Act 2016) to keep pace with changing telecommunications technology and enforcement practice.

section_titles: Source:** UK Statutory Instrument, in force from 26 December 2017
text:
**Link:** https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/radio-equipment-regulations-2017

These Regulations set out the technical and safety requirements that radio equipment (including marine VHF sets) must meet before they can legally be placed on the UK market or put into service. They were originally made to implement the EU's Radio Equipment Directive (2014/53/EU) into UK law and have since been adapted for the UK's post-Brexit UKCA (UK Conformity Assessed) marking regime, distinct from the EU's CE marking.

The Regulations' "essential requirements" (broadly in regulation/Article 3) require that radio equipment be constructed so that it protects the health and safety of users and other people (including domestic animals) and property; that it achieves an adequate level of electromagnetic compatibility, meaning it neither causes excessive interference to other equipment nor is itself unduly affected by interference; and that it makes effective use of the radio spectrum so as to avoid causing harmful interference to other radio users — a point directly relevant to why "unnecessary transmission" and "non-standard phrases" on VHF are discouraged, since spectrum efficiency is a legal design and use consideration, not just an etiquette one.

The Regulations place obligations on the various "economic operators" in the supply chain — manufacturers, importers, and distributors — including duties to prepare technical documentation, ensure conformity assessment procedures are followed, cooperate with enforcement authorities, and withdraw non-conforming equipment from the market if concerns are identified. Ofcom has powers to evaluate and act against radio equipment that presents a risk. The Regulations exclude certain categories of equipment from their scope, including some radio amateur and marine equipment governed by separate regimes, and they allow for different requirements in Northern Ireland reflecting its distinct post-Brexit trading arrangements.

text:
**Source:** International Telecommunication Union (ITU), a United Nations specialized agency
**Link:** https://www.itu.int/pub/R-REG-RR

The ITU Radio Regulations are a binding international treaty — technically an integral part of the ITU's Administrative Regulations, which complement the ITU's Constitution and Convention — governing how the global radio-frequency spectrum (from 9 kHz to 300 GHz) and satellite orbits are used and shared among all 193+ ITU member states. They are the foundational document underpinning virtually all national radio law, including the UK's Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006.

The Regulations are revised roughly every three to four years by the World Radiocommunication Conference (WRC) to keep pace with new technology and changing spectrum demand, with the most recent full edition dated 2024. They are published in four volumes: Volume 1 contains the Articles (definitions, technical terms, and substantive rules, organized into chapters and numbered provisions); Volume 2 contains the Appendices (including detailed technical annexes such as those governing distress and safety frequencies); Volume 3 contains Resolutions and Recommendations; and Volume 4 contains ITU-R technical Recommendations incorporated by reference.

Of particular relevance to VHF maritime use, the Regulations define and classify various maritime radio services — the "maritime mobile service" (communication between coast stations, ship stations, and onboard units), the "maritime mobile-satellite service," the "port operations service" (restricted to messages about the operational handling, movement, and safety of ships, explicitly excluding general public correspondence), and the "ship movement service" (similarly restricted to messages about ship movements). This is the direct legal source for the PLA bulletin's requirement that VHF transmissions be strictly relevant to safety of navigation and operational coordination — the ITU treaty itself defines these radio services narrowly and excludes casual or personal messages from them by treaty definition. The Regulations also govern priority of communications (distress and safety traffic takes precedence), secrecy of communications, and the allocation of frequency bands (via the Table of Frequency Allocations in Article 5), which nationally-administered plans such as the UK's must follow.

**Source:** International Telecommunication Union (ITU), a United Nations specialized agency
**Link:** https://www.itu.int/pub/R-REG-RR

The ITU Radio Regulations are a binding international treaty — technically an integral part of the ITU's Administrative Regulations, which complement the ITU's Constitution and Convention — governing how the global radio-frequency spectrum (from 9 kHz to 300 GHz) and satellite orbits are used and shared among all 193+ ITU member states. They are the foundational document underpinning virtually all national radio law, including the UK's Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006.

The Regulations are revised roughly every three to four years by the World Radiocommunication Conference (WRC) to keep pace with new technology and changing spectrum demand, with the most recent full edition dated 2024. They are published in four volumes: Volume 1 contains the Articles (definitions, technical terms, and substantive rules, organized into chapters and numbered provisions); Volume 2 contains the Appendices (including detailed technical annexes such as those governing distress and safety frequencies); Volume 3 contains Resolutions and Recommendations; and Volume 4 contains ITU-R technical Recommendations incorporated by reference.

Of particular relevance to VHF maritime use, the Regulations define and classify various maritime radio services — the "maritime mobile service" (communication between coast stations, ship stations, and onboard units), the "maritime mobile-satellite service," the "port operations service" (restricted to messages about the operational handling, movement, and safety of ships, explicitly excluding general public correspondence), and the "ship movement service" (similarly restricted to messages about ship movements). This is the direct legal source for the PLA bulletin's requirement that VHF transmissions be strictly relevant to safety of navigation and operational coordination — the ITU treaty itself defines these radio services narrowly and excludes casual or personal messages from them by treaty definition. The Regulations also govern priority of communications (distress and safety traffic takes precedence), secrecy of communications, and the allocation of frequency bands (via the Table of Frequency Allocations in Article 5), which nationally-administered plans such as the UK's must follow.

---

section_titles: Source:** International Maritime Organization, Resolution A.918(22), adopted November 2001
text:
**Link:** https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/Safety/Pages/StandardMarineCommunicationPhrases.aspx

The SMCP is a standardized set of English-language phrases developed by the IMO to reduce the risk of misunderstanding in verbal maritime communication, given that English is the internationally recognized working language at sea but is not the first language of most seafarers. It replaced an earlier, narrower document called the Standard Marine Navigational Vocabulary (SMNV), which had been in use since 1977.

The SMCP is organized into two parts. Part A covers essential phrases for external communication (ship-to-shore, shore-to-ship, and ship-to-ship) as well as onboard communication, focusing on navigation and ship handling — this is the part formally required for certification purposes. Part B is a supplementary, non-mandatory set of additional phrases intended to support wider maritime English learning. The phrases cover both routine situations (such as berthing and pilotage) and standard responses for emergencies, and are deliberately built on a simplified subset of English grammar and vocabulary to minimize ambiguity.

Under the STCW Convention (the International Convention on Standards of Training, Certification and Watchkeeping for Seafarers), officers in charge of a navigational watch on ships of 500 gross tonnage or above are required to demonstrate the ability to understand and use the SMCP as part of their certification. While the SMCP is primarily aimed at bridge-to-bridge and bridge-to-shore navigational safety communication rather than being a VHF-specific procedural rulebook, it is the natural companion to the PLA bulletin's requirement for clear, concise, and standardized language on VHF, since ad hoc or idiosyncratic phrasing is precisely what the SMCP was designed to eliminate.

---

text:
**Link:** https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/mgn-324-mf-amendment-2-navigation-watchkeeping-safety-use-of-very-high-frequency-vhf-radio-and-automatic-identification-system-ais

MGN 324 (M+F) is MCA guidance directed at owners, masters, officers, and pilots of merchant ships, nautical training institutions, and owners/skippers of fishing vessels, yachts, and pleasure craft. It has been reissued and amended several times (the current version is "Amendment 2"), each time in response to continuing marine casualties in which misuse of VHF radio was identified as a contributory factor.

Its central message is that although VHF radio can be a useful aid to avoiding collisions, it must never be allowed to override or substitute for compliance with the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea 1972 (COLREG) — in other words, a VHF conversation agreeing on a course of action between two vessels does not override the formal collision-avoidance rules, and over-reliance on VHF negotiation to resolve close-quarters situations has itself been a cause of accidents. The Note reiterates that marine VHF equipment must be used strictly in accordance with the ITU Radio Regulations described above.

The guidance also addresses the Automatic Identification System (AIS), clarifying that although AIS is not explicitly referenced in COLREG, it can usefully improve situational awareness for identifying ships, tracking targets, and gathering additional information. It cautions watchkeepers, however, that not all vessels carry AIS (particularly small leisure craft, fishing vessels, warships, and some shore stations), and that AIS may in some circumstances be legitimately switched off at a master's discretion — so officers of the watch should not treat the AIS picture as a complete or fully reliable representation of surrounding traffic. Taken together, the Note positions VHF and AIS as supplementary situational-awareness tools that must be used within, not instead of, the established rules and procedures for safe navigation.

---

text:
**Source:** Office of Communications (Ofcom)
**Link:** https://www.ofcom.org.uk/manage-your-licence/radiocommunication-licences/ships-radio

This is Ofcom's guidance on the licensing regime for radio equipment carried on ships, covering medium frequency (MF), VHF, high frequency (HF), and ultra-high frequency (UHF) radio equipment, as well as satellite communications, radar, Emergency Position-Indicating Radio Beacons (EPIRBs), and Search and Rescue Transponders (SARTs). The stated purposes of licensing are twofold: to prevent radio equipment from causing undue interference to other users of the spectrum, and to ensure equipment is operated only by competent, appropriately trained individuals.

Historically a UK "Ship Radio Licence" required annual renewal and a fee, but following a 2005 Ofcom consultation and policy change, ships' radio licences became "lifetime" licences from 1 October 2006 — free of charge, issued electronically, with no fixed expiry date, remaining valid as long as the registered details stay accurate (though licensees must periodically reconfirm their details). A licence is personal to the licensee and does not automatically transfer if a vessel is sold. Separately from the equipment licence, the individual operating the radio needs an operator's qualification — for VHF-only use this is the Short Range Certificate (SRC), obtained via a one-day training course covering radio procedure, etiquette, and use of Digital Selective Calling (DSC); a Long Range Certificate (LRC) is needed for other, longer-range communications equipment.

Operating marine radio equipment without both the required ship licence and a valid operator's certificate is a criminal offence. Ofcom's enforcement team can issue on-the-spot fines, and the maximum penalty on conviction is a £5,000 fine and/or up to six months' imprisonment, with the possibility of forfeiture of any radio apparatus used unlawfully. This is the direct legal underpinning of the PLA bulletin's warning that improper VHF use may lead to penalties enforced by Ofcom.

text:
Professional VHF communication follows structured patterns that ensure message clarity while reducing transmission time and preventing channel congestion during busy maritime operations.

Essential communication elements include:
► Station identification: Clear vessel name and call sign identification
► Message markers: Instruction, advice, warning, information, question, answer, request, intention
► Standard responses: Affirmative and negative acknowledgments with full repetition
► Position reporting: Precise location using degrees, minutes, and geographic references
► Time references: UTC notation with clear hour and minute designations

Example (Initial Contact):

Vessel A: "Port Control, Port Control, this is MV Ocean Star, 
call sign Hotel Alpha Bravo Charlie One, on Channel One-Two. 
How do you read me? Over."

Port Control: "MV Ocean Star, this is Port Control. 
Reading you loud and clear. Go ahead. Over."

International phonetic alphabet usage ensures accurate information transmission when spelling becomes necessary during radio communications. Standardized number pronunciation prevents confusion that could result in navigation errors or operational mistakes.

section_titles: ► Standard Marine Communication Phrases are mandatory for of
text:
► Standard Marine Communication Phrases are mandatory for officers in charge of navigation watch on vessels over 500 gross tonnage
► Message markers must precede communications to clarify intent: instruction, advice, warning, information, question, answer, request, intention
► Phonetic alphabet uses specific pronunciations like ZEERO for zero, WUN for one, and FOWER for four to prevent transmission errors
► Position reporting requires degrees and minutes with cardinal directions, avoiding decimal degrees for radio communication
► Time references must use UTC notation clearly stating hours and minutes to prevent timezone confusion
► Emergency communication hierarchy progresses from MAYDAY (distress) through PAN-PAN (urgency) to SECURITE (safety)
► VTS communications require accurate vessel information including dimensions, cargo details, and operational restrictions
► Pilot communications address boarding arrangements, safety equipment, and weather conditions before transfer operations
► Weather reporting follows meteorological standards using cardinal points for direction and Beaufort scale for wind force
► Bridge team communication requires systematic information sharing with clear command acknowledgment procedures

How To Talk On A Marine VHF Radio [Radio Etiquette]
By

text:
What is the correct way of talking on a marine VHF radio? You must use the proper channel for the given situations, communications must follow protocol, and the right language and terminology must be used for every transmission.

A key aspect of being at sea is safety. A VHF marine radio is a means of communication for all situations, particularly emergencies.

And in urgent situations, the last thing you want is for your calls to be lost in translation.

Talking on a VHF marine radio requires you to use the correct channels relative to your needs and know how to communicate your location. Using appropriate vocabulary, knowledge of the NATO (phonetic) alphabet, and following step-by-step protocol for conveying messages is vital.

When using VHF radios for marine communication, finding a channel, tuning in, and starting a conversation is not straightforward.

Below, I will explain the correct procedure, the language and terminology used while talking on a marine VHF radio, the appropriate channels, and what is considered bad etiquette.

Contents (TLDR)

How Should You Talk On A Marine VHF Radio?
First of all, you should be aware of who can use a marine VHF, and then you can follow protocol for VHF radio comms at sea.

This is true for emergencies and other communication. The steps are listed below for non-emergency-related communications.

How Should You Talk On A Marine VHF Radio?
First of all, you should be aware of who can use a marine VHF, and then you can follow protocol for VHF radio comms at sea.

This is true for emergencies and other communication. The steps are listed below for non-emergency-related communications.

[1️⃣ Identify Your Needs — definition]
Why are you trying to establish communication? Even for non-urgent matters, you must know the best and most concise way to verbalize your needs via marine VHF radio.

text:
Who are you trying to communicate with? This may be another vessel, the marina, or anyone else in the vicinity with a VHF radio.

You also cannot make a general call to anyone in particular and hope for a response. This is not only bad etiquette but also an incorrect procedure. A call must be made to a specific station or vessel.

[2️⃣ Identify Your Point Of Contact — definition]
Who are you trying to communicate with? This may be another vessel, the marina, or anyone else in the vicinity with a VHF radio.

You also cannot make a general call to anyone in particular and hope for a response. This is not only bad etiquette but also an incorrect procedure. A call must be made to a specific station or vessel.

text:
Use VHF channel 09 to establish initial contact, and be sure to use the correct contact call sign. Be sure to repeat their station name three times, followed by “this is” and your vessel’s name, and end by saying “OVER” and wait for a response.

When contact has been made, move the conversation to the “working” channel and continue.

📻 Example: “Port Royal, Port Royal, Port Royal. This is The Black Pearl. Over”

[5️⃣ Communicate Your Needs — reference]
Communicate your needs with the other contact clearly and use the correct terminology, call signs, numbering, and NATO alphabet if required.

text:
Make the location of your vessel known. An approximate location can be given by providing distance and bearing from the nearest landmark.

If you have a GPS, then provide your contact with the coordinates. Exact coordinates only need to be provided in an emergency situation. If moving, then give your heading and your speed in knots.

Communication may be slow or stagnant in some instances. If no further response or contact has been made after fifteen minutes, return to channel 09 and repeat the process until a stable line of communication has been established.

[SECTION BREAK]

When conversing with the contact, provide any further information required by the other vessel or enquire about anything that needs further clarification from your end.

text:
After you have made contact and communicated your needs, you are free to set sail as you were.

How To Make An Urgent Or Emergency Call On Marine VHF Radio
Distress or emergency calls made on marine VHF radios can change the predicament that you may find yourself in for the better or worse.

Follow the steps below to ensure that your call gets heard, understood, and responded to in time:

1️⃣ Identify the type of emergency you are in. Will you be using “Mayday,” “Securité,” or “pan-pan”? These terms are clarified in the table further down.

2️⃣ Tune your radio to channel 16

3️⃣ Repeat your signal three times. (e.g., ” Mayday. Mayday. Mayday”)

4️⃣ Next, follow with “This is” once, and your vessel name repeated three times.

5️⃣ State your position or location

6️⃣ State what kind of situation you are in (e.g., sinking)

7️⃣ Clarify how many people are on board the vessel and also if any require medical attention

8️⃣ Specify the kind of assistance you would need.

9️⃣ Say “over” once you are done communicating your requirements, but stay near the radio for as long as possible.

🚨 Example of a distress call: “Mayday! Mayday! Mayday! This is The Black Pearl, The Black Pearl, The Black Pearl. I am 5 miles east of Davy Jones’ Locker. We are sinking. Seven people are on board. Over.”

section_titles: 🗣️ Marine VHF Lingo: What It Means And When To Use It
text:
Specific words, codes, phrases, and numbers must be utilized while talking on a marine VHF radio.

Speaking over the radio in your everyday vernacular will confuse people and will likely not be taken seriously. Furthermore, you could end up with a citation or a fine.

Specific Words To Use While Talking On A Marine VHF Radio:

Mayday: used for distress calls. Only to be used in grave and imminent danger.
Pan-pan: used for potentially dangerous situations but not yet at “mayday” level.
Securité: used to alert and bring attention to nearby boaters of something. Such as urgent marine information broadcasts.
Affirmative: used instead of “yes.”
Negative: used instead of “no.”
WILCO: used to say “will confirm.”
Roger: indicative of agreement and compliance
Over: indicates the end of the transmission message
Hear/ read/ copy: shows that your transmission has been heard
Stand by: end transmission, but continue to monitor channel
Repeat: repeat the last transmission
The NATO Alphabet And How To Use It On A Marine VHF Radio
When required to spell out something, the traditional ABCs you learned in school will be useless here.

At sea, the NATO alphabet is utilized with “I spell” prefacing the word. So, for example, if you were to spell out “whale,” the communication would go as follows: “I spell Whisky, Hotel, Alpha, Lima, Echo.”

The same applies to any letters of the alphabet that need to be relayed. “A” would be Alpha, “B” would be Bravo, and so on.

The Proper Way To Communicate Numbers Over Marine VHF Radio
The numerical system only goes from 0-9 in maritime communications. Therefore, numbers above 9 will be conveyed by first saying “figures” and then the individual numbers.

So if you wanted to say 35 (thirty-five), it would be said as “figures three five.”

text:
13	Bridge to bridge	When one vessel needs to communicate directly with another ship.
16	International distress	Used for emergency situations only. 
1022 (formerly 22A)	Coast guard liaison	Restricted to use by the US Coast Guard. You can receive weather and storm warnings here.
68 	Non-commercial working channel	An example of a working channel is where vessels will move communications after making contact through 09 or 13.
Channel 09 is not to be used for conversational purposes. Instead, it is there to make initial contact after you move to a working channel, such as 68.

You can also check out The United States National Cast Guard’s complete list of channels and what they are used for.

section_titles: Bad Etiquette When Talking On A Marine VHF Radio
text:
Being at sea is a risk within itself. It is, therefore, important that the rules of maritime communication are respected and adhered to.

Communicating via marine VHF radio is no exception. The items listed below are considered bad etiquette and can lead to the perpetrator being fined.

Swearing. Keep in mind these channels are open and can be heard by anyone.
Not releasing the push-to-talk button.
Using casual language or language that does not follow marine protocol.
Not monitoring emergency channels and other important ones for the area.
Having a casual conversation on an emergency or working channel.
Making a fake distress call.

chapter_title: 09 Commercial and non-commercial boaters calling When trying…
text:
How Do You Call A Coast Guard On VHF?
Try to remain calm
Turn your radio channel to 16
Say “coast guard” three times, followed by “this is” and the name of your vessel
State your location
State your emergency
Describe your needs
📢: The Coast Guard can only be contacted in an emergency or urgent situation.

How Do I Make A VHF Call?
1️⃣ Switch on the VHF unit and adjust the “squelch” until there is no more static

2️⃣ Do a radio check, but not on emergency channels. “open channels” such as 68, 69, and 72 can be used for radio checks.

3️⃣ Repeat “radio check” three times, followed by the name and location of your vessel.

4️⃣ Await confirmation from another station that your call has been heard and that your VHF radio is in working order.

5️⃣ Proceed to use the correct channels and terminology to communicate your needs.

You can also check out the YouTube video posted by Sailing Vagabond Epicurean featuring an interview with a US Coast Guard outlining basic procedures and information.

What Is A Push-To-Talk System?
Push-to-talk communication refers to a system whereby a button needs to be pushed to switch between voice reception and voice transmissions. This is a two-way communication mode, but only one person may speak at a time.

Understanding and using the correct terminology at sea is vital in boating, especially when communicating with other vessels via marine VHF radios.

Remember the most important channels for emergencies (09, 16, 1022) and the terms you would use for each situation.

If you would feel more comfortable having a “cheat sheet” of numbers and terms near your VHF radio, then, by all means, have one!

Be sure to brush up on the NATO alphabet, register your VHF radio, and familiarize yourself with the terminology so that your transmissions are copied loud and clear!
